subsubtopic: NEED FOR DISCUSSION WITH COMPANIES AND UNIONS TO OBTAIN REASONABLE INTEREST RATES AND PRICES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing necessity.
Considering that the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity stated in an article published in La Presse on February 7 last that salary demands denote a sharp upward trend; considering that a report financed by the Economic Council of Canada also published last week indicated that chartered banks had made excessive profits of $500 million from 1968 to 1973 and that this trend is continuing, since one of them increased its profits by 58 per cent in its last financial year; considering finally that those trends could signal a new inflationary push, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That this House enjoins the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to initiate immediately some discussions with corporations and unions to make them moderate their interest rate, selling prices or wages demands, as the case may be.

I would draw to the minister's attention a statement made in this House yesterday by the Minister of Finance who stated: "The government has concluded that the power of inquiry was needed by CSIP, but as we could not give this power to CSIP we created a new institution". subsubtopic: DEFICIENCIES IN COMMUNICATIONS AND OPERATIONAL PROCEDURES AT UNCONTROLLED AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. It arises from Transport Canada's committee report on operational interface which was concluded in June, 1976. The committee reported that there were very serious deficiencies in communications and operational procedures at Canada's uncontrolled airports. It advanced some positive recommendations and urged that they be implemented immediately.
The committee further stated that the severe procedural problems were only symptoms of a deeper, fundamental problem which required a solution of national scope. I ask the minister why he and his department have failed to react to this report expeditiously and why they have failed to carry out the recommendations contained therein. Why was the report buried? Why has the minister not seen the report? If he has, why have communications' regulations not been amended to reflect the recommendations in the report?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board

Action was taken on that report to begin development procedures. The report concentrated particularly on areas where there might be many different radio contacts in one zone. Certain procedures were looked at. Therefore, the hon. member is quite wrong in suggesting there was any burying of the report. Actually, it began to be developed in this regard, as it did in regard to other uncontrolled airports, following the report.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subtopic: WHEAT-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN PRICE PAID TO WESTERN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. It is asked on behalf of the wheat farmers in western Canada. On December 18 last, I raised an application in the House under Standing Order 43, asking that consideration be given to paying an additional 50 cents a bushel to farmers on the delivery of their wheat. If you look at Hansard for that date, you will see that it was turned down by Liberal members, including the Minister of Transport.
In the past few days, on the way to Damascus, the government decided to pay the extra 50 cents a bushel that I asked for in December and which was turned down at that time. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. A report published by the C.D. Howe Institute in December claimed that figures supplied by Statistics Canada are inaccurate, misleading and hastily contrived.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege as a result of remarks made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) last week in my absence in the course of what he called either a question of privilege or a point of order. Apparently it was prompted by the motion raised under Standing Order 43 by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) regarding confidentiality of tax information. Somehow my name was brought into this matter.
In attempting to assess what the minister was alleging in my absence and the weight to attach to whatever it was he was trying to express, I checked Hansard respecting the most recent question of privilege prior to this one where the minister rose to explain he no longer intended to write memoranda to himself, confidential or otherwise. No doubt the minister was referring to those which somehow escaped his office and were reported widely in the press that illustrated among other things his fixation with trying to get out of the shadow of his cabinet colleague, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). He and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce share responsibility for the confidentiality of income tax forms, and so far he seems much more willing to accept the responsibility.
When this so-called point of order involving myself was raised by the minister on February 27, as reported in Hansard, Your Honour said the following:
The record will have to be examined. My memory is that the minister in his intervention said that the hon. member for Central Nova was possessed of stolen documents. That was the language used; at least, that is my recollection. Like the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), I will examine the record, as I am sure the minister will, to see whether he made an accusation of a member having committed an offence. If he did, that will have to be withdrawn. We will have to examine the record. The minister, of course, is on notice to that effect.
The following day, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), according to Hansard, defended the Minister of National Revenue by claiming the minister had never said that I "had stolen those documents or knew that the documents were stolen". He concluded by indicating that there was absolutely nothing wrong in that statement, and he asked Your Honour to set any question of privilege aside.
In examining the record of the House, I have found that the Minister of National Revenue, in spite of his self-confessed determination to acquire a reputation of being "a nasty piece of goods" and a "target for animosity", did not claim I had stolen the income tax returns in question. In fact, he said that I was "possessed of stolen tax returns". As I have mentioned already, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council, presumably speaking for the government, assured the House the minister has never claimed that I knew the documents were stolen.
I am quite willing to accept this assertion from the government benches, and I do not wish necessarily to pursue this

March 6, 1979
Privilege-Mr. MacKay
particular point any further. However, I must remind Your Honour of the fact the minister on the same occasion, as reported at page 3632 of Hansard, accused me of "revealing these forms to the public". I suggest this is not only false but highly objectionable. The simple fact is that confidential income tax information which came into my possession was never made public by me.
The quote from the Globe and Mail story of February 23 indicated that I showed copies of four 1974 tax returns. In the House the minister was wrong again and referred to them as 1977 tax returns "with social insurance numbers, taxable income, income tax paid and spouses' names in full view". Your Honour will note that I took care to see that taxpayers' names were obliterated, while those responsible for the care and custody of the tax returns through their carelessness allowed the forms to be left lying around with all the details clearly visible. Then the Globe and Mail story continued:
The Nova Scotia M.P. said he would not release the names on the returns. He said some have already been destroyed but he would not say where the others are.
It is clear I took precautions with the confidential material sent to me. On a confidential basis I even sent a letter to the minister responsible for Statistics Canada, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, indicating that some of his constituents were affected. For this reason I ask the Chair, having regard to the precedents in Beauchesne's fifth edition under "unparliamentary remarks" and having regard to Your Honour's fine dissertation on a question of privilege raised on March 22, 1976, to extract a withdrawal from the minister if Your Honour thinks it is proper.
I have just about come to the end of my brief presentation, but since this matter was raised in the connotation of the law being broken, and with some suggestion that I was involved in it, I should like to say that there may very well be some instances of the law having been broken. If so, it requires investigation to see whether the persons in Statistics Canada who, as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce very properly said, have a responsibility to ensure that these highly confidential documents are kept inviolate, have not been in breach of the obligations under the statutes, particularly section 23, 18 and 16 of the Statistics Act.
The Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) took a very laudable position when the matter was first raised. As reported at page 3473 of Hansard, the minister said:
Mr. Speaker, of course I agree there is a responsibility to protect the confidentiality of information provided to the government, particularly the confidentiality that is prescribed by law. It is the responsibility of the government to ensure that the law will be carried out.
Before I make a motion on this matter, and by way of additional information which I intimated to the hon. Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, indeed there is evidence previous ministers and officials were warned in writing that there were appalling conditions regarding the lack of security in the very building, over ten years ago, where these income tax forms were found. If I may, I will read one sentence to

illustrate the point. This is information made available to the Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin back in 1969. It reads:
In 1968, when the Health and Welfare Division at DBS moved to No. 5 Temporary Building, some mental morbidity cards were stored in room 2141, (although a vault was available a few feet away); more current cards were kept as before in unlocked filing cabinets ... A few flimsy cardboard boxes, lids open, containing notifiable disease cards were also kept in this room.
This is the point: it existed over ten years ago. It continues: Any person, a tramp... or someone with more deliberate intent, might easily stroll into the rooms where cards were kept when civil servants were off duty, at night or on weekends, and examine these cards.
In view of these longstanding abuses which I have brought to the attention of the minister today and which he indicated he would look into, I should like to make the following motion:
That the confidentiality and security procedures of income tax forms, made available by virtue of the Statistics Act to Statistics Canada, be referred to the appropriate parliamentary standing committee to determine the adequacy of existing procedures under the Statistics Act and the regulations thereunder pertaining to confidentiality of income tax matters.
I remind the House and the Chair that in the current information being supplied to Canadians regarding their income tax forms under the Canadian Human Rights Act the following is included:
An objective of Revenue Canada Taxation is to maintain public confidence in the integrity of the tax system. To achieve this objective the Income Tax Act stipulates that the information you provide on your income tax return must be kept strictly confidential.
Sir, I think this matter is sufficiently important that it should transcend any petty bickering about who said what to whom and ought to be referred to the appropriate standing committee. Obviously, if there is no trust in the tax system of this country, the whole system is in jeopardy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same question, and I rose before the minister spoke because I felt there was another very narrow point that should be dealt with in determining the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay).
If I read the record correctly, and if I heard the hon. member correctly, the minister's words were that "the hon. member for Central Nova was possessed of stolen documents". That was the phrase, and that, sir, is a criminal offence. The possession of stolen property is a criminal offence under the Criminal Code. Therefore, the charge that the hon. member for Central Nova was in possession of stolen documents suggests that he is guilty of a criminal offence.

subtopic: REFER SECURITY PROCEDURES TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: No.

March 6, 1979

This is a charge of the commission of a criminal offence, and being that the minister should withdraw. I think you, sir, should deal with that specific point. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFER SECURITY PROCEDURES TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Before recognizing the minister I should point out that I think we find ourselves in a bit of a procedural difficulty here in that the motion put forward for consideration by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) is not in fact a motion which relates to his grievance in the question of privilege, but is a substantive motion which relates to an examination of the confidentiality of income tax returns. That in itself is a very important matter. The hon. member obtained the floor on a question of privilege which relates to some remarks by the minister, but the motion which he would introduce, while relating to that subject, is not in fact a complaint against the language of the minister.
On the other hand, the point made by the hon. member for Central Nova, and referred to by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), is a valid point.
Let me go back to the intervention by the parliamentary secretary, which is a correct statement, that in fact simple possession of documents that may have been or were stolen is not in and of itself a criminal offence. However, in that regard we are getting very technical. The hon. member, incidentally, said at the beginning of his remarks that he took that intervention as meaning that it was not intended that he be indicted in that way by the minister's remarks.
However, the hon. member for Central Nova then went on to make another point, namely that he did not divulge or reveal this information, and the revealing of that information would be an offence.
On both counts I think we ought to leave this matter very clear. The word of the hon. member in this case must be accepted by hon. members of this House-that is to say, there was no guilt involved in the possession of the documents themselves-and the hon. member's word must be accepted that he did not reveal the information, thereby committing an offence. We cannot deal with this matter without establishing that. However, the hon. member has compounded the case, it seems to me, by ending his remarks with a substantive motion, not one of privilege.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. C. Abbott (Minister of National Revenue and Minister of State (Small Business)):
subtopic: REFER SECURITY PROCEDURES TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a moment or two, because of the seriousness of this problem, to deal with the question of taxation documents and why they may be in the hands of Statistics Canada. During the course of this intervention there have been allegations made from various quarters that Revenue Canada has been slipshod in the handling of these documents and that Statistics Canada should not necessarily have the documents.
The point I would first like to make is that Statistics Canada has an obligation to provide facts, collect statistical
Privilege-Mr. MacKay
information, and provide, among other important facts, the earnings by society of income and its distribution.
The tax returns of individuals and corporations which are provided to National Revenue for purposes of tax administration provide the best and most reliable source of information on incomes. Parliament recognized this in section 23 of the Statistics Act when it stated:
The Chief Statistician or any person authorized by him to do so may inspect or have access to any returns, certificates, statements, documents, or other records obtained on behalf of the Minister of National Revenue for the purpose of the Income Tax Act.
At the same time, parliament was concerned that the information so provided to Statistics Canada should be kept confidential and, therefore, it further provided that the "information when communicated to Statistics Canada shall be subject to the same secrecy requirements to which it was subject when collected". Clearly this means that employees of Statistics Canada are required to comply with the severe confidentiality provisions of the Income Tax Act which imposes penalties upon an official or authorized person who shall knowingly communicate or allow to be communicated any information obtained for the purposes of the Income Tax Act.
Statistics Canada publishes income information only about groups in a way that hides tax information about any individual. Those are the provisions of the law, provisions of the Income Tax and the Statistics Act, and my department and Statistics Canada, to the best of my knowledge, operate in accordance with these provisions.
We now come to the point raised by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). He refers to my position the other day, that I was concerned that members were making wide ranging allegations that income tax information, not simply in the hands of Statistics Canada but perhaps also in the hands of Revenue Canada, were being handled in a slipshod manner. I attempted during the question of privilege to assert that this was not the case and that a good deal of the blame for this whole incident rests with the hon. member for Central Nova.
In an article in the Globe and Mail of February 23, which I did refer to earlier on the question of privilege, the hon. member revealed that he had gone to Statistics Canada and had found about 50 cardboard boxes full of confidential tax returns which he said were "lying unattended in a Statistics Canada office building in Ottawa". The duties and responsibilities of the hon. member as a parliamentarian do not give him the right to go into a building which he may say is improperly guarded and under the guardianship of Statistics Canada, to go down to the basement of the said building and look at files in boxes which are marked confidential, return and presumably, if this article is correct, encourage others in the form of news cameramen or others to take the same journey and photograph the boxes and whatever documents may be there.
The hon. member, knowing the law, knowing the obvious security provisions of the Income Tax Act, and knowing that he himself had seen the boxes marked "confidential", received,

March 6, 1979
Privilege-Mr. MacKay
he asserted, 100 or so returns. Ele showed a Globe and Mail reporter copies of four 1974 tax returns he had been given, the taxpayers' names having been obliterated, but with the social insurance numbers, the taxable income, income taxes paid and spouses' names in full view. The article goes on to state:
The Nova Scotia MP said he would not release the names on the returns. He said some have already been destroyed but he would not say where the others are although he promised he would eventually destroy all the forms he had been sent.
He knew perfectly well that he was not entitled to copies of those forms. He knew they were bound by the Income Tax Act, and he knew that whoever had communicated them to him had done so not only improperly but unlawfully. When, indeed, I suggested he was possessed of stolen reports, I had no doubt that these returns, if transmitted to him anonymously or otherwise, had been transmitted by someone acting outside his right under the law and who was committing a serious offence. Naturally, knowing the hon. member's zeal for justice and his inquiring mind, his instincts as a detective-we all remember the bugging caper of not so long ago-he recognized that he had a self-appointed duty to ferret out such matters.
Certainly I was not accusing the hon. member of any criminal offence because he had those documents in his possession, for many people, perhaps disgruntled people, know him as a likely source of interest to whom such information could be sent. Nor do I stand and say that Statistics Canada, in the instance the hon. member revealed, was managing the documents with the kind of care which is required under the law. I think that my colleague the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) confirmed this somewhat when he said that the law had to be obeyed but that it was because of financial shortcomings that they could not properly look after the documents. I do not think that this is a reasonable excuse. Statistics Canada must obey the law and look after such documents with great care.
At the same time, however, I think that I was right in taking the position back to the hon. member himself that he had gone to a building, that he knew the records were highly confidential, that he only raised the point because of this high confidentiality and the legal requirements for secrecy and that he brought the matter before parliament and the news media and showed them returns in a fashion, according to the report, that any intelligent observer could find out to whom the returns belonged. For example, the report stated that some of the returns were from Alberta farmers. There was a picture taken, thanks to the guidance of the hon. member who led the media to the premises of Statistics Canada, which shows the form of a resident of Courtenay, B.C. The name was obliterated from the picture, but it was taken.
I suggest that the hon. member did not act with the kind of responsibility which one should expect of a member of parliament in such circumstances. He seems to have done so only for the purpose of gaining the centre of attention by leading his crew of cameramen around so that he could be photographed in his self-appointed role as guardian of our society. When

I stated that that information was stolen I suggest that clearly I am correct. The hon. member had no business having that information in his hands. It should not have been transmitted, anonymously or otherwise, by the person or persons who did so, and it is a serious offence under the law. I suggest also that the hon. member acted with a good deal of recklessness in encouraging reporters to take a look at the documents he had in his hands and in encouraging other media representatives to take a tour of Statistics Canada's building to see other tax returns.
I do not feel that there is a question of privilege here. If I had accused the hon. member of stealing documents, of course, I would have been wrong and would have quite properly been obliged to withdraw the remark; but I do think that anybody could assert that the 100 income tax documents which were marked highly confidential and which were in the hon. member's hands, having been sent to him anonymously, could have been sent to the hon. member by anybody who was doing anything but stealing that information as defined under the law.
I am not suggesting that the hon. member is guilty of a criminal offence because he held on to those documents. Perhaps in his position as a member of parliament he has certain rights in the interests of the public to deal with the matter and acknowledge his possession, I do not know. What I suggest is that there is no question of privilege, and 1 believe that my position in this matter is entirely conscionable.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFER SECURITY PROCEDURES TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the facts as they have been asserted in terms of the status of the document which the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) received-using the words of the minister, "documents that must have been stolen"-are correct, then I do not think that the minister has obliterated of defended the question of privilege which has been raised by the hon. member. In fact, what he has done is compounded the position of the hon. member for Central Nova. The minister's words, "possessed of stolen returns" in reference to the hon. member for Central Nova are damaging to the hon. member. It is also a tenet of the criminal law that the doctrine of recent possession casts an onus upon a member of parliament or anyone else in whose possession those documents are found to turn them over to the proper authority.
The question of necessity under those circumstances takes on a different aspect. What the minister has done in making the statements he has, instead of admitting perhaps overzealousness in his desire to be the cutting, controversial figure and arguing that there is no question of privilege, is in fact established grounds for a question of privilege. The House cannot allow this to stand. The word "stolen" casts aspersions on the honesty and integrity of a member before the House, and it cannot be allowed to stand.
If the hon. member's motion is imperfect in the manner in which it is put, we have had imperfect motions before and time has been given to perfect those motions; and I think that it is the duty of the Chair to allow that time.
March 6, 1979

It is an offence within the law that applies to income tax officials, Statistics Canada officials, private citizens, members of parliament or whoever, to break the confidentiality which is imposed upon them.
In the second reference the words "and this private dick in residence in the Tory party has been revealing these forms to the public" constitute an accusation by the minister to the effect that the member for Central Nova has committed an offence.

subtopic: REFER SECURITY PROCEDURES TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Those are his own words.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFER SECURITY PROCEDURES TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not think that those words should be allowed to stand. There is no question of intent there, and the words themselves raise a question of privilege. The hon. member for Central Nova ought to have time, if he has been imperfect in his motion today, to make the necessary corrections.
The final matter which I want to deal with is the question whether a member of parliament has a duty in a public building. For the purpose of my argument, I do not put a member of parliament in the position of trespassing on such property, which is the implication. Unless a member of parliament went into a building against the instruction of the security service guarding that building or against some form of indication on the building that he could not enter, then a member of parliament or anybody else can go into that building and go through it. There is nothing sacrosanct about a government building unless it is made sacrosanct.

subtopic: REFER SECURITY PROCEDURES TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: There better not be.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFER SECURITY PROCEDURES TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) has said, there better not be. Supposedly, we operate a relatively open system. However, there is a duty on the Government of Canada, which was accepted by the government House leader last week, to maintain certain confidentiality.
If there has been a breach of that duty of confidentiality, then the public will judge the circumstances and conduct themselves accordingly with regard to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) or the minister responsible for Statistics Canada, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, or whoever, as to what credit ought to be bestowed upon them for maintaining confidentiality. In these circumstances and according to the minister's own admission, there is not very much credit to be bestowed.
Unless a member of parliament is stopped-he is no better or worse than any other citizen in society-that member has the right to go into a public building. As I understand the situation, the hon. member for Central Nova was allowed into this particular building and into an unsecured area to look at documents, with the media present, by the security service. This is an indication of the respect for confidentiality-and that is the important issue-that the government has in these circumstances.
Privilege-Mr. MacKay
I do not think it lies in the mouth of the Minister of National Revenue to try to point the spear at the hon. member for Central Nova, nor does it lie in his mouth to argue as he did that an accusation with respect to an offence-two offences at least-ought to be allowed on the record of this House. The important part of this argument is not who is right or wrong; the question is that the minister, as a gentleman, ought to have withdrawn the remarks he made and he did not do so. I think he ought to be made to do so.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFER SECURITY PROCEDURES TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Order, please. I am faced with a fundamental difficulty that seems to have been overlooked. I am not worried about the part which refers to a public building as that seems to me to be peripheral to the main issue.
Procedurally the matter of the hon. member's motion has perhaps a reduced significance. The hon. member was seeking by his motion to investigate the handling of confidential documents in the income tax department. If that is going to be done it ought not to be done by way of a question of privilege related to some remarks by the minister.
The minister has said today in his place, however stridently he has done it, that "I do not accuse the member for Central Nova of the commission of an offence. The documents which he had in his possession which he has acknowledged were documents unlawfully obtained." That is the opinion of the minister; he is entitled to that opinion and he is entitled to express it.
In respect of the possession of the documents he said, "I say those documents were stolen." The minister maintains: "They are unlawfully obtained, therefore I say stolen, and the member for Central Nova was in possession of those. 1 do not accuse the member of the commission of an offence." It seems to me he added another phrase: "Perhaps the member sees himself in a role as an elected member as having some rights in respect of that."
This question has come up before in respect of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt) when he was being pursued on a regular basis over a period of time to return documents to the House which he had in his possession and about which he had given some information. It was contended at that time that the status of those documents was clear-they were unlawfully obtained and the member had them ir. his possession. The question therefore became one of some interest as to what are the rights of a member who is in possession of these kinds of documents that have been brought to him when he looks at the documents and knows that they are confidential and that they are not being handed to him by the person in whose care they belonged. It seems to me there was more than an allegation in that case; there was an acceptance of the fact that the member was in possession of documents which were unlawfully obtained.
In the case before us it seems to me that the minister has said virtually the same thing. The hon. member for Central Nova, in his capacity as a member of the House of Commons, came into possession of documents which, on looking at them,

March 6, 1979
Privilege-Mr. MacKay
appeared to be obtained irregularly. In fact, the minister says that, in his opinion, they were stolen, clearly. He does not accuse the member for Central Nova of any complicity in their theft and in fact allows that the member may consider himself to be the logical possessor of such documents if it helps him to bring a grievance against the government which he may see as part of his duties. That remains a very open, legal question. The minister has said today that he does not accuse the member for Central Nova.
I think the minister is entitled to his opinion that the documents have been unlawfully obtained, is entitled to regard the fact that the member for Central Nova had them in his possession and he is entitled to say so. He has to make it clear that he does not accuse the member for Central Nova of any offence and he, in fact, has said that.
The question of privilege of the hon. member in attempting to get to an investigation of the confidentiality of documents is irregular. It does not conclude the same way it began. What remains is the question of whether the minister has made unparliamentary remarks about the member for Central Nova.
I have had to conclude that in respect of the commission of an offence, the minister has said he does not accuse the member of an offence regarding possession of these documents. The member took that, and I think correctly, to mean that he was not accused of an offence in the possession of those documents. In fact, he may consider that confidential documents may be brought to a member of the House of Commons in some way by a person who, as the minister said, may consider himself disgruntled or otherwise in order to air a grievance. That remains, to me, an unresolved legal question. I have to accept the conclusion that the minister is entitled to say that without accusing the member of an offence, and in fact he made it clear that he did not accuse the member.
There remains one other item, however, and that is that the hon. member for Central Nova had behaved in a manner in which he revealed the contents of those documents to the public. That is an offence. Therefore, if I am to be consistent and the minister in his remarks used language which indicated the hon. member was reckless in his duties of one thing and another, I want before concluding this matter to have the same clear position from the minister, if I may, on behalf of the decorum of the House, that he is not accusing the member for Central Nova of an offence in respect of the information contained in those documents. Then I think procedurally we can put the matter to rest.

subtopic: REFER SECURITY PROCEDURES TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I quoted only from the Globe and Mail, which was the source of my information in this case, and indicated that the hon. member for Central Nova had shown the reporter copies of four 1974 tax returns, etc. I did not accuse him because I was quoting only from a newspaper report which, however consistently reliable that publication may normally be, none the less could be in error. I am simply saying that if that was the case-and the hon. member did not deny it-then I found it offensive. It is not an offence, I guess, but I found it offensive.
If Your Honour feels that I am charging an offence improperly, then we will clear the record. I did not accuse the hon. member of an offence. I said that presumably by his own acknowledgement he showed certain forms to a newspaper reporter who published the fact, and I found that offensive. I do not say he committed any offence in doing so.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFER SECURITY PROCEDURES TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not know that the matter can be any more clear in terms of parliamentary language. I do not think that procedurally we need to pursue the matter any further.
Had the question of privilege of the hon. member been related, in a motion albeit imperfect, to remarks of the minister, I think we would have perfected it. I think he has gone one step further, however, in attempting to introduce a substantive motion to investigate the confidentiality of documents in the possession of a department. This is a bit of a leapfrog over the substance which is contained in his motion. These two matters of possibly unparliamentary accusations by the minister did remain. I now find that the minister has withdrawn both. If any such allegations were made by the minister they are now withdrawn. The matter is therefore closed.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROPRIETY OF MOTION UNDER S O. 43 MOVED BY HON. MEMBER FOR ALGOMA
MR. NIELSEN-PROPRIETY OF MOTION UNDER S O. 43 MOVED BY HON. MEMBER FOR ALGOMA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question of privilege arising out of today's question period. It concerns a question which was asked by the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster); I am sorry to see he has left the House. He has asked questions on the same subject in times past. As you know, he is the chairman of the Standing Committee on Northern Pipelines.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROPRIETY OF MOTION UNDER S O. 43 MOVED BY HON. MEMBER FOR ALGOMA
speechtext: Order, please. I do not think the hon. member was recognized in the question period. He presented a motion pursuant to Standing Order 43 before the question period.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROPRIETY OF MOTION UNDER S O. 43 MOVED BY HON. MEMBER FOR ALGOMA
speechtext:
That is right. Thank you for correcting me on that, Mr. Speaker. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, chairmen of standing committees have a very particular position, one that is closely analogous to that of parliamentary secretaries. When Your Honour first assumed your duties as Speaker you were very quick to state your view that you were not going to recognize parliamentary secretaries for the purpose of asking questions because of the special relationship they enjoyed with ministers, and particularly you would not recognize parliamentary secretaries asking questions of their own ministers.
Today we have the chairman of a standing committee, who is more knowledgeable than non-committee members, asking questions with political intent, in my view to gain ground only, concerning a subject matter about which he is very knowledgeable and based also on the fact that he enjoys a special relationship with the minister responsible for pipeline affairs. He is the only chairman I am aware of who is following this course.
I do not submit that it is improper for chairmen of committees to ask questions concerning matters not falling within their responsibility. That happened today when the hon.

March 6, 1979

member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), the chairman of the public accounts committee, put a question to the minister which had no bearing on his responsibilities as chairman of that committee. The chairman of the Standing Committee on Northern Pipelines also has a party responsibility, if not an official responsibility, to keep the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) informed of the progress in committee and the matters discussed therein.
I believe that allowing the chairmen of standing committees to question the ministries for which they are responsible is just as offensive and an abuse of the accepted practice of the House as being allowed to put motions under Standing Order 43, or to ask questions of those ministers.
Incidentally, that committee is sitting this evening at eight o'clock. The content of the motion that the hon. member put under Standing Order 43 was based on evidence which is currently being given and has been given before the committee. The committee, as you know, sir, has not yet presented any report to the House. I submit that that is an offence. It is not within the rules to base a motion on evidence given to a standing committee before that committee has reported to the House. It is just as offensive for a question to be put.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROPRIETY OF MOTION UNDER S O. 43 MOVED BY HON. MEMBER FOR ALGOMA
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROPRIETY OF MOTION UNDER S O. 43 MOVED BY HON. MEMBER FOR ALGOMA
speechtext: It is my submission that the evidence before standing committees prior to those committees reporting to the House cannot be raised in the House. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you are familiar with that rule. If need be I can turn it up very quickly.

speakeroldname: Mr. Yvon Pinard (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROPRIETY OF MOTION UNDER S O. 43 MOVED BY HON. MEMBER FOR ALGOMA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the hon. member is mistaken because he confuses committee with department. The chairman of a committee is not the parliamentary secretary to a minister; that is obvious. But, if in practice parliamentary secretaries to ministers are not allowed to put questions in the House, as you stated specifically in one of your rulings, Mr. Speaker, it is doubtless because the Parliamentary Secretaries Act stipulates, very simply and very tersely, that parliamentary secretaries help the minister as requested by him. However, no law or House rule stipulates directly or indirectly that the chairman of a committee must be muzzled either in the House of Commons or in committee.
Mr. Speaker, the remarks of the hon. member stand up even less under close examination because they do not concern a situation where the chairman of a committee put a question to the minister, which would have been perfectly in order, but it does deal with a situation where the chairman of the committee acted through a motion presented pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 43 of our House.
Privilege-Mr. Nielsen
Now, if I am not mistaken, you yourself, Mr. Speaker, have recognized that a parliamentary secretary can present a motion under Standing Order 43. All the more so if a parliamentary secretary, like the one sitting on my right, has already done so-the parliamentary secretary to the minister of urban affairs at the time was recognized-so, if a parliamentary secretary can present a motion under Standing Order 43, the chairman of a committee can also certainly present that type of motion. Nothing in our traditions, regulations or laws prohibits this.
Finally, on the hon. member's remarks concerning what is said before a committee, may I remind him that as a rule committee meetings are deemed to be public. There is therefore no harm in repeating in this House, be it by the chairman or any member of the committee, the evidence brought before the committee, be this done by means of a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 or questions to ministers, or even in any debate on a motion or otherwise. Nothing forbids the chairman or any member of a committee referring to revelations made before a committee holding public meetings.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I think the question raised by the hon. member is a little far-fetched. He referred to absolutely no regulations, laws, customs or traditions to support his point.
I would therefore ask you to simply reject his contention.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROPRIETY OF MOTION UNDER S O. 43 MOVED BY HON. MEMBER FOR ALGOMA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when you rule on this point, perhaps you should also tell us what it was in our proceedings this afternoon that stopped all the clocks.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROPRIETY OF MOTION UNDER S O. 43 MOVED BY HON. MEMBER FOR ALGOMA
speechtext: I intended to keep the House up to date at least on that matter. It is now exactly 3.45 p.m. Hopefully before the end of the day we will reactivate the clocks on the floor.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROPRIETY OF MOTION UNDER S O. 43 MOVED BY HON. MEMBER FOR ALGOMA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise briefly on the same point of order. It would seem to me that if the arguments of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) were true, they would also apply at this particular juncture in our history to the chairman of the public accounts committee who happens to be a member of the official opposition. That would mean, of course, that when the public accounts committee is examining the public accounts, the chairman of that committee would not be able to address questions to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan). It would also mean that when the Auditor General's report is before the committee on public accounts he would not be able to address questions to any particular minister whose department was under review by that committee at that time. He did just that.
It seems to me that such action would be a curtailment of the rights of members on that side or on this side of the House. In my opinion, the hon. member's point of order is not a point of order at all but simply an argument that he has put forward, for whatever reason I do not know.

The House resumed from Monday, March 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet that Bill C-29, to amend the National Housing Act and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act and to make other related amendments, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, when I called it ten o'clock last night I pointed out that there were just a few more things I wanted to say on this matter. I cannot help but wonder whether the fact the clock has stopped is somewhat symbolic of what is happening in parliament in these closing days. It may by symbolic of how much is being accomplished.
I began my remarks last night by referring to the speech made just prior to mine by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier). There was a great deal that he said with which I agreed. One such comment was recorded in yesterday's Hansard at page 3832, and I quote:
I know the minister cannot control everything going on in these projects, rehabilitation projects, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation projects and others where you have to qualify and where qualifying means being a Liberal.
When he said that, I did a double take. My memory took me back almost five years to the summer of 1974 when it came to my attention that there were some CMHC housing projects in my constituency. One in particular had been built by a developer under the general umbrella organization known as Imperial Ventures with head office in Winnipeg. The head of that organization has added something to his record. He is not only the former Liberal leader of the Liberal party in Manitoba, but the former Liberal leader of the former Liberal party in Manitoba. His organization known as Imperial Ventures built a project called low dividend housing. That was a good idea on the part of the former leader. The program was supposedly to provide houses for low income families. The government loaned money to the developer at a low interest rate, presumably because the profit on that investment would not be in the rental but on the appreciated value of that property. It was a good idea.
It came to my attention that some of the rules for that kind of housing were not only being bent but broken. There are certain strict rules which CMHC officials impose on a venture like that. I took it upon myself to visit the project. One of the rules was that you had to have a family. Second, you had to be
March 6, 1979

below a certain income level. Obviously you had to require that kind of housing. I presented myself to the manager of that project. There were no questions asked about whether I had a family or what my salary was at the time. There were no qualifying questions at all.
I started probing and asking certain questions. I found out that on the bottom floor of the department block were the single bedroom apartments. On the second floor were smaller apartments or family units and on the third floor were the three bedroom apartments. When I asked whether it was necessary to have a family to move in there, I was told it was not necessary at all. I asked what was done about people who did not have families but wanted to rent an apartment on the third floor. I was told that there were career people who rented those. They divide the rooms among themselves. These are several adults occupying one suite. If a couple without a family rented a three bedroom apartment, I was told they would make the third bedroom into a den.
This was a project for low income families. In no way were the rules being adhered, to. The manager was not ensuring that those who needed housing the most were the ones to benefit from that project. The former Liberal leader of the former Liberal party in Manitoba has done very well by this project even to this day.
As the hon. member for Roberval pointed out last night, we cannot blame the minister for that. I do not hold him accountable. As the hon. member for Roberval said, the federal government should never have been involved in this kind of program. It is a centralist notion. It is from a bygone era when a lot of people in Canada, particularly members opposite, thought that the central government could solve most problems in Canada. My colleagues and I did not think so.
We found out through the affairs of this department that that is far from being possible. There is no government agency omniscient enough to be able to supervise all of the building projects and investments that CMHC has made across Canada. There is no one agency that can ensure that the rules are not being broken. When guidelines and rules are set up to protect low income families, they are broken. This means that those who need housing the most are being ripped off.
Therefore, I am happy to see this legislation which will do away with the department of housing and urban affairs. I am glad the government has accepted our proposal and said yes, it is time for this department to be disbanded. I commend the government for taking this initiative and being able to turn over to the provinces some of the projects that belong to provincial areas, letting those governments do as they should have done in the first place.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I participate in this debate. As the housing critic of this party, I will be summarizing the approach this party is taking to the measures proposed by the minister and the government as well as looking at the housing situation in general. From listening to the minister's remarks some ten days ago and from reading the speeches of Liberal
Housing
members who participated in this debate, one would not recognize that there is a housing problem in Canada.
The minister and his associates trot out figures showing that over 200,000 houses are being built each year. They say there really is no housing crisis in Canada today. The minister spent a great deal of his time assuring hon. members that there is no problem with housing, that what is needed is a bit of tinkering here and there, such as the amendments being put forward, in order to clear up the problem that he says exists.
I have often thought that many members of parliament and many governments live in a cloud in cuckoo land. The minister occupies one of his own rather uniquely. I invite him to come to my constituency in Toronto and tell the people there that there is no housing crisis in the city of Toronto and no housing problem in Canada today. I am sure it would come as news to many people.
Who are these people? It is not the rich who are concerned. It is not only the people we classify as poor. It is many people starting out, with one income and sometimes with two incomes, who 20 or 30 years ago would have found it easier to buy a house even though the standard of living at that time was lower than it is today.
I follow the remarks of my colleagues the hon. members for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) and Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) in saying that Canadians are house poor. The high cost of housing is shattering the Canadian dream. It is not part of this party's policy that everyone should live in a single family dwelling or that everyone should live in an apartment, but that people, regardless of their income, should be able to live in affordable, decent shelter. Those who want to live in houses should be able to do so. Those who want to own their own homes should be able to do so. Those who want to own their own homes should be encouraged to do that.
It is more difficult for Canadians to own their own homes now than it was 20 or 30 years ago. Right now, the average price of a house in metropolitan Toronto is $68,500, and it is anticipated the price will rise by a further 7 or 8 per cent over the coming year. In many parts of Toronto, in the central core, for example, prices have risen to about $80,000. With mortgage rates at a high of 11 'A per cent the dream of being able to afford one's own home is becoming unattainable.
It is important that we should look carefully at the causes of the extraordinary inflation which has taken place in this area. What are the components which go into the cost of housing? In all the research the government has sponsored and all the work of CMHC, very few studies have been undertaken which tell the truth about the reasons for the present high cost of housing. It is a monument to the government's political ability that it has managed to convince itself, on the basis of only the Lord knows what information, that there is not an "affordability crisis" in the cities of Canada today. Look at the costs which have gone up. We admit that the cost of labour has gone up. One can see that the cost of materials has risen; this was

March 6, 1979
Housing
documented by my hon. friend from Sault Ste. Marie when he talked about the price of lumber and so on.
But the price increases do not stem solely from increases in the cost of labour and materials. They are caused by two other factors-the cost of money and the cost of land. When you look hard at what the government has done to protect Canadians from the increasing price of money, you find the answer is "not a single thing". Quite the reverse. They have encouraged interest rates to rise to a point at which it is impossible in Toronto to get a first mortgage for less than 11 per cent or a second mortgage for less than 13 per cent. We all know that increasingly it takes two mortgages to enable a family to acquire a home.
The cost of land is the other factor which must be closely examined. In our view, land should be considered a resource just as we consider oil or coal or gold to be a resource. Precisely the same phenomena as we have seen with respect to the exploitation of other natural resources-domination by foreign companies, a tendency for greater concentration, control over the price of the products-are being repeated in the case of land. We in our party have argued that we can see a pattern developing-a greater concentration taking place in the economy leading to excessive profits and consumer gouging. We can see this happening with regard to the price of land.
So we have "an affordability problem". More than one million Canadians are paying over 30 per cent of their income for shelter. We have a serious interest rate problem which is forcing many families into permanent and uncontrollable debt. Also within the housing industry there is the situation in which fewer and fewer companies are controlling land, not only in the inner cities but in the suburban areas. We know the names of these companies-Cadillac-Fairview, Genstar, Trizec. Such firms are accumulating land around the cities, controlling the choices which are available and restricting the ability of our people to afford decent housing.
What is the major lesson to be learned from this? First, any housing policy which fails to deal with the large developers and the powers of financial institutions cannot possibly succeed because it is these two groups which are the major source of the problem. Proposals such as those put forward by the Conservative party, and put forward as well, though admittedly in a striptease, delicate fashion, by the minister of state for housing and which simply increased consumer demand without dealing with inflation and profiteering in the supply of housing, serves simply as a guarantee of higher prices and higher profits. To put it crudely, if you simply put money into the hands of consumers without doing anything about the supply of housing or the cost of money, you are merely supplying a subsidy to developers and bankers.
The second lesson to be learned is that any subsidy on housing and home ownership should be clearly expressed and costed. The Canadian people should be allowed to see exactly who would benefit from any change in subsidy and at what price. I find it ironic in the extreme that the parties which have been advocating restraint at the expense of working Canadians

should now be proposing solutions costing billions of dollars like some nineteenth century evangelist who had suddenly discovered the sins of the flesh.
Third, we should be crystal clear as to the full extent of any subsidies both from the point of view of the direct expenditure of public moneys and also from the point of view of what we call tax expenditures. Tax expenditures have aptly been called hidden welfare, and we are still in the dark as to the cost, for example, of capital cost allowances and accelerated depreciation provisions under the Income Tax Act.
Then there is the cost of tax shelters from multiple unit residential buildings known as MURBs, tax deferrals which allow companies to withhold taxes in a given year and put them off on a continuing basis; and there are the tax provisions which have just been put forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) which will allow for the continuing write-off of all carrying charges on undeveloped land.
In addition to action along the lines of the three points I have made, something else has to be done. There is an obvious need for tax reform which would bring relief to lower and middle income Canadians. It is increasingly difficult, I would stress once again, for the average Canadian to afford to buy a house and live in affordable housing or in an affordable apartment. A government which does not take note of this fact will find itself facing some unpleasant music when it finally realizes it has to call an election.
Finally, there is no instant or magic solution to the problem of affordable housing. If there is no free lunch, as the Liberals and Tories are so prepared to say when they discuss unemployment insurance and direct government expenditure, there is no free lunch in tax spending on housing either, and that is something that both the Liberals and Conservatives would have the Canadian people believe. The hard fact of the matter is that fewer and fewer developers control the supply of land. Private land banking has replaced public land assembly, and we have no control over the price of land. To increase demand willy-nilly when so few companies control the supply of land is simply an incentive to profiteer. House prices will not simply rise, they will go through the roof.
That is the background against which we have to consider the housing proposals that have been put forward by the government. It is the background of ever increasing concentration of wealth, of control over the supply of land; it is the background of ever increasing corporate power, private power and control by the public; the background of ever increasing mortgage rates and extraordinary bank profits. Of course, the final story is the high price of a house.
It is against this background and not the cloud cuckoo land in which the minister lives that we have to consider the Liberal party's proposed amendments to the National Housing Act, because the thrust of the amendments is to reduce public control and public investment in housing. But there is one problem, and that is that while the government would have us believe that it is leaving the housing situation to the so-called
March 6, 1979

free market, the fact of the matter is there is no free market in housing.
I want to quote from one CMHC report which was published surreptitiously, one might say, and which exposed the high cost of land in 1976. Peter Spurr says the following about metropolitan land development:
Metropolitan land development has been taken over by the giants, who are now consolidating their position by buying up their competition, and the suppliers and materials in their production processes. The small builder, revered in the mythology of housing, is an anachronism-the residential construction industry in metropolitan Canada can be recognized as paralleling the structure of the automobile industry during the 1920s, or the aircraft industry in the 1940s. The understanding of this reality could lead to several different objectives for public policy, ranging from the break up of the evolving cartel, to the nationalization of the firms, to increased public supervision of their products and prices. Of the three, the latter seems most directly related to the quality of life and substantive needs of this society.
That was the suggestion and recommendation of Mr. Spurr who wrote the report for the government on the high cost of land and land prices. What did the minister in all his wisdom, and the people who are advising him in CMHC, do? Did they decide to break up the cartels? The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) has been looking for a backbone for four years and he still has not found one with respect to the competition policy. Have they nationalized land or done anything about public control or ownership of land? No. Have they done anything about public supervision of products or prices? No, they have specifically refused to do so. They have gone from one impotent institution to another in their attempt to find an answer to the problem of inflation, not only in housing but in the rest of the economy, and they have not come up with a single answer. Now they are desperately trying to find a political solution to save them when they come to call an election.
What has been the answer? They have rejected each of the three possibilities put forward by Mr. Spurr, and now they have come with a fourth one. It is called "leave the jungle to the lions". It calls for a reduction in public involvement in housing, a reduction in the kind of control that is available, and it leaves it all to the private sector. This would come as no surprise to us because the government and the Liberal party, which have made millionaires of Campeau and Teron, of Cadillac-Fairview and Trizec, of Genstar and Daon, are now fulfilling their historic mandate to make Canada even safer for the development industry than it has been up to now.
We will have occasion, when the bill goes to committee- and we will see what committee it goes to, depending on the attitude of the government-of looking at the proposals in detail. Some of them have been dealt with by my colleagues the hon. member for Winnipeg North and the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie. But I want to make one point. I am sorry the minister is not here to hear this, but perhaps he will have the opportunity to read it. My point is that in the pre-election period in which we are living now the government is attempting to put the gun to the head of the opposition and to say: "We have to have the housing bill passed". They have done it with every other piece of legislation with which they have
Housing
come up. Each one is a matter of urgency. They say they need to have the unanimous consent of the House to get it through.
Let me say this to the minister. He has delayed the bringing in of this bill and yet he is the one who allowed the neighbourhood improvement projects to lapse and left them hanging in mid air, with the people involved not knowing what was going to come next. He is the one who allowed his deputy minister at this critical time to take an extensive leave of absence and now to quit the government for good. He is the one who announced in May proposals which were opposed by many of the groups affected by these proposals, and it took him until November before he could get agreement from those groups to the amendments he was putting forward. He is the one who waited until December to have the bill printed the second time, and his government was the one responsible for waiting until February before they decided to bring this bill in. They are the ones who are responsible for the delays, the costs, the abandoned projects and the defeated hopes. It is not us but the government who are responsible for this delay and this extraordinary mismanagement.
There are hundreds, not to say thousands, of groups affected by the changes in the government housing program. 1 can only mention one from my riding in the short time I have been here. There is a project in my riding of which the minister is aware because 1 brought it to his attention a number of times. The project is for a senior citizens' building which is in danger of languishing-it is a non-profit corporation-because this government has delayed and has refused to give direct government funding to groups which are in need as they wait for the introduction of this new policy.
The basic thrust of the new policy has to be seen in light of the announced cutbacks of over $300 million in the CMHC budget in August and September. The government is determined to get out of a number of areas and to leave them to banks, to the private sector and to trust companies. We have no guarantee that the private sector and the trust companies are interested in supporting co-ops or are interested in supporting non-profit corporations.
The government has introduced the graduated payment mortgage scheme, which is a fraud on the Canadian public, and I say that with no apology whatsoever. I want to quote from the "Graduated Payment Mortgage Safari Kit" which was provided to the members of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs by the minister in December. This kit was supposed to explain to us the great benefits of the graduated payment mortgage scheme. What does that scheme do? It allows a potential home buyer to pay a lower total amount of money in the first four or five years of his mortgage, and then requires that he pay an escalated amount of his mortgage after the first five years. The key fact, which is not mentioned once in this GPM safari kit, is that the total amount of money which an individual would pay is greater over a 25-year amortization period than it would be under an equal payment mortgage, which is what we have in Canada today. It is unbelievable that that fact is not mentioned once in a government document presented to members for briefing.

March 6, 1979
Housing
If a private group put forward this proposal and did not provide an explanation, they would be guilty of misleading advertising of the worst kind and would be prosecuted by the government. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs should have a look at this document. It is a clear example of the kind of thing many lenders in the private sector would like to get away with, that is, concealing the true cost of a loan from the consumer. Now we know why the government is afraid to bring in an act to protect creditors and borrowers. It is because the government does not want to reveal the true cost of loans to Canadians.
If the Liberal party is bankrupt, I should like to look briefly at what we have heard from the Conservative party. Apart from criticism, applauding the government for abolishing the ministry of urban affairs and for giving its role back to the private sector, the only proposal put forward by the Conservative party was one to allow the deductibility of mortgage interest and property tax from pre-tax income. I admit this proposal deals superficially with one of the problems I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, and that is the problem of tax relief. Obviously one would pay less tax, and it would provide a substantial saving to a large number of Canadians.
The main problem with the scheme is that it does not do anything about the problems facing the housing industry and Canadians who are interested in buying houses. It does not do anything about high prices, corporate concentration, or creating equity between home owners and tenants. It is a massive hidden subsidy of home ownership at the expense of the rest of Canadians. In political terms it can be compared to those nineteenth century Conservatives who opposed giving the vote to non-property owners. What twentieth century Conservatives are saying is that Canadians who are not lucky enough to own property will not receive the benefit of a tax cut. The Tories are barring nearly 40 per cent of Canadian households from the benefits of economic citizenship.
The hon. member should say that in the trade union halls.

I have said this wherever I go. I admit the scheme provides a form of tax relief, but I do not think it provides the Conservative party with a monopoly on virtue. It is a proposal which creates inequities between home owners and tenants. It means the government will spend millions of dollars in the subsidization of a particular group. The fact it is a hidden subsidy and may be superficially politically popular is irrelevant. Nevertheless it is a subsidy. It does nothing about the key housing problems facing Canadians. It is a tax relief which provides relief to some but not others. We in the New Democratic Party are interested in tax relief. Certainly we are interested in the problem of cost relief, but our approach will not be at the expense of some Canadians and to the benefit of others.
Our approach is based on two premises: affordability and fairness. It is time to look very hard at the groups in our society who have prevented Canadians from having the type of

housing they deserve. Since 1945 huge amounts of Canadian investment capital have been absorbed in urban development. With the guarantee of the federal government, financial institutions recognized a safe market and invested heavily in this sector. In 1977 the total value of real estate mortgages outstanding was $73.9 billion, far more than the total federal budget. Since 1945 the government has allowed this distortion to grow in our economy. The economic policy of the federal government has allowed more money than was needed to be used in the development of urban real estate. From 1945 to 1977 the amount of money spent on urban real estate by Canadian financial institutions increased 100 times.
What has been the effect? The effect has been to suck money from many of the productive and manufacturing sectors of the economy into speculation and urban land development. While some sectors of the economy have done well, such as urban land, other sectors have been underfed, underplen-ished and starved by the lack of capital and investment. Also it is important to recognize what has happened with the massive profits made in urban land and real estate.
Rather than investing in the industrial sector of Canada, our dollars are flowing south into the United States. The investment of Canadian capital in the United States is being led by real estate companies. The workers and the people of this country who are looking for jobs are being bled dry by the investment going out of the country.
For example, Markborough Properties and the Meridian building group announced plans in May, 1978, to finance a portion of a $1 billion new town in Dade County, Florida. Olympia and York Ltd. of Toronto bought eight New York City office buildings for approximately $350 million. Cadillac-Fairview holds close to $200 million in current United States real estate assets. Genstar, a foreign-owned company, has been dominant in the Canadian real estate industry. Now it is exposing its tentacles elsewhere in North America. Recently it acquired Westmor Corporation of Long Beach, California, which owns mortgage bank branches in Georgia, Nevada, Arizona and California. Also it bought 8,600 acres in San Diego for $93 million. This flow of capital south draws money away from Canada. Profits generated in Canada should be used for the benefit of Canadians.
The same trend can be seen elsewhere in the economy. Inco has made money at the expense of the workers in Sudbury and the people of that community for a decade. Now it is investing its profits in Guatemala and Indonesia. The same pattern of dependence, exploitation and the exporting of jobs and wealth is going on in the urban and real estate sectors.
We in the New Democratic Party feel the price of land must be controlled, as well as profit speculation and cost of money. In order to deal directly with the housing problems facing Canadians, those matters must be controlled. Our attitude toward land must change. Land should be seen as a resource which needs the protection of public policy. It is too valuable a resource to be left solely in the hands of private developers. The entire development industry was created from the idea
March 6, 1979

that urban land and buildings are private property which should be used, owned and developed by the corporate sector.
But urban land has been and always should be considered as one of Canada's natural resources. It provides a basic need- shelter. The need for shelter should not be subject to profiteering. We cannot allow land to be taken off the market and held by a developer until he or his company feels the land will bring the desired price. We should provide encouragement to the non-profit, co-operative and municipal sectors of housing. The leading builder in Toronto today is the city of Toronto. I am proud to say that city has had the guts and ability to get into the housing market. It has attempted to deal with the high cost of housing in its own way.
In relation to public land assembly, our proposal has been rejected consistently by the government. We need to reduce the cost of mortgages. That has been the proposal of my party since 1973. Mortgage rates are too high; bank profits are astronomical.
Why does the government not have the ability, guts or integrity to deal with these problems and put them together in a very simple equation? I think the people of Canada would be behind the government if it said to the banks: "Do something about mortgage rates and take the cost out of excess profits".
We need amendments to the Bank Act and to the National Housing Act not only to allow the government to offer mortgages at 8 per cent, but to force banks to do the same for Canadian families that are earning less then $25,000 a year. This is not a public subsidy. We are not the last of the big time spenders, like the Conservatives and Liberals seem to want to be with their tax exemptions and allowances for the people. This is something that will be coming from the banks' excess profits which have been hurting the people of Canada. Let us not forget that bank profits last year were $1 billion. Let us not forget that a good part of this, according to information provided to us by the banks themselves, is simply a windfall produced by increasing the spread between the Bank of Canada rate and the banks' prime rate. Such a windfall has even been admitted to by major spokesmen of the banking community, as I have said.
I do not see why the banks should be allowed to benefit, and I do not see why we as taxpayers and interest payers-and we are all taxpayers and interest payers; certainly I am-should continue to allow ourselves to subsidize these monuments of marble and glass when we cannot affort to buy adequate housing for our children. The Bank of Canada's attitude toward restraint is perhaps best revealed by the building it has just constructed for itself across the way.
Should we not start talking more of the waste and excess profits and misuse of our social resources? The difference in monthly payments between a mortgage of $50,000 at 11 'A per cent and a mortgage of $50,000 at 8 per cent is over $100 a month, or $1,200 a year which could be going back into the pockets of the Canadian people, not at the expense of their brothers, some home owners or another taxpayer, but at the
Housing
expense of those people who have been living off the backs of the Canadian people. That is a significant saving.
This government should deal with mortgage interest rates, problems in relation to profits and significant savings. It should not go round the circle and brush aside the problem, but should get at the heart of the matter. The heart of the matter is the fact that interest rates are too high, bank profits are too high and land costs are too high.
If the government wants to deal with these problems directly, then it should deal with them directly by assembling land and providing it at no profit to the Canadian people. I think the slogan for the voting public in this election year should be "let the buyer beware". It would be easy enough for us in this party, as the other parties have done, to play the game of cheque book politics. Cheque book politics will not necessarily solve problems in housing. We have seen what the Tories have proposed to buy votes. I think I said earlier in a speech outside this House that rather than buying votes, the Liberal party only wants to rent them, and that is the proposal it has been putting forward. This is a strategy that has been followed by the minister. He says we might have a tax shelter, and we might do something about our unfair tax system that will be of benefit to more than 30 per cent of the people, but on the other hand we might not. This government does not even have the courage to propose something and let the people decide. The fact of the matter is that buying votes will not make it easier for one single Canadian to buy a house. That is the key to the problem. We need to keep the cost of land down and we need to keep the cost of money down. I say, why not take the bull by the horns and do it directly?
