speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Bill C-29 is a carefully prepared and thought out response to the housing situation as it exists in Canada today. It is quite obvious, as has been mentioned many times, that Canadians are among the best housed people in the world. For that reason it becomes even more important to address ourselves to the needs of those people among us who still have problems in getting access to housing that is appropriate to their needs and within their means.
The new non-profit and co-operative housing programs set out in this bill are a practical and workable solution to the problem of generating housing for low income people at an affordable cost. I am particularly pleased that these programs, more than ever before, will involve the private sector of the economy in the provision of social housing. There is no reason that social housing should be the exclusive responsibility of government, and it seems apparent that private investors are now willing and desirous of becoming involved.
Under the non-profit and co-operative programs, and by several other parts of this bill, private lenders will be allowed to provide capital in projects which up until now were financed from government resources. That policy is consistent with the relationship the government has always encouraged between the private and public sectors.
The government is not in the business of constructing houses. The most efficient and economical way to get houses built is by private enterprise within a free and competitive market economy. When the private marketplace is working as it should, most Canadians will be able to deal with their own housing problem. That is why an important part of the government's participation in housing has been devoted to encouraging the maintenance of a healthy housing industry in Canada.
Mortgage insurance was introduced soon after the end of World War II to encourage private lenders, particularly banks, to increase their investment in residential construction, to make more money available to finance the building of housing at a time when mortgages did not seem to be such an attractive kind of investment. That one program, mortgage insurance, has probably dome more than any other measure to establish and maintain a healthy housing market. It has been modified from time to time to conform with changing needs.
In recent years the government has followed the pattern of introducing publicly funded and supported housing programs and then, as they became familiar and acceptable, modifying

them in such a way as to permit them to be supported by the private sector. Two notable examples have been the assisted home ownership program and the assisted rental program which initially involved both federal government loans and federal government subsidies to put good housing within reach of people who needed it.
Those two programs were among the most successful and popular ever introduced. These programs were later modified, first, to permit them to be financed with private capital rather than government loans and, second, to replace government subsidies with a system of repayable, interest reducing loans. The logical extension of this pattern is the new graduated payment mortgage, a private loan which allows borrowers to make lower payments during the early years when they are getting established in a new home.
I am not suggesting that the private sector of the housing industry should be expected on its own to take care of all the housing needs of all Canadians. The Government of Canada through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has always had an important role to play, in partnership with private enterprise, to ensure that Canadians have good housing at affordable cost.
There are two ways in which the government will continue to fulfil that obligation. One way is to provide subsidies for the construction and acquisition of housing which fulfils a social need. This bill provides for generous assistance to non-profit groups and co-operative associations that are prepared to make housing available to people who need it. This assistance will be provided in a way that eliminates overlapping administration by various levels of government and allows the provinces to fulfil their own objectives according to their own priorities in an area that is essentially within provincial jurisdiction.
The second way in which the federal government interacts with the private sector to ensure adequate annual production of housing is through the mortgage insurance program. When we ask private investors to make money available for social housing, or for rehabilitation, or through the graduated payment mortgage, we encourage them to do so by making mortgage insurance available.
This bill extends the benefits of mortgage insurance to a number of new situations not previously covered-for instance, mortgage loans to non-profit organizations for the acquisition and improvement of existing housing; for loans to landlords who are prepared to rehabilitate their rental properties to acceptable standards of health and safety; and, for the first time, for housing loans to Indians living on reserves.
One of the most encouraging aspects of this legislation is that it strengthens the partnership between government and private enterprise in the housing industry, making the best possible use of the resources of each sector. This housing legislation gives further support to the provision of housing to people of low income. I am referring to co-operative housing, which has become increasingly popular in recent years as Canadians have come to understand and accept the idea of
March 6, 1979

collective action to solve individual housing problems. The co-operative movement in housing had to overcome many obstacles before receiving the recognition it is given today. It is now considered to be an important alternative approach to meeting low-income shelter needs.
Support for co-operative housing is another indication of federal adaptation to new situations and shifting demands. Canada in 1979 is not the same as the Canada of 1946, and the National Housing Act is not the same instrument it was 30 years ago. At that time the primary task was to rebuild a housing industry that had been virtually closed down by the priorities of a country at war.
The changes since then have been dramatic and comprehensive. It was recognized at the outset that relying on the free market system for the production of housing does not automatically assure an equitable distribution of that production. Without a degree of government intervention, lower income households could face the problem of either spending a large portion of their income to obtain adequate and suitable shelter or paying lower rents for inadequate and unsuitable shelter. As a result, housing legislation over the years has responded to two primary needs: to assist families who were in need of housing but had affordability problems; and to assist builders to supply an adequate volume of good, moderately-priced housing.
An important change in social policy was marked in 1949 when the act first incorporated provisions for public housing. At that time CMHC contributed 75 per cent of the cost of construction and the province paid 25 per cent. The project was owned in partnership by the federal and provincial governments and operating losses were shared on a 75-25 per cent basis.
Just 15 years ago, in 1964, the act was again amended to give the provinces another option in providing housing for low income families. The new provision called for CMHC to make 90 per cent loans to provinces and municipalities to provide public housing. Provinces paid the remaining 10 per cent, and operating losses were shared by the federal government and the provinces on a 50-50 basis. During this time and, in fact, up until 1973 co-operative housing was treated as just another form of home ownership and received the same treatment and benefits as a single applicant for a home owner loan.
1 might point out that there are two types of housing co-operatives. One is called the building co-operatives, in which a group of people simply pool their resources to build their housing at the same time, with each member of the group owning his unit outright. A continuing co-operative, on the other hand, is a non-profit group that provides housing for its members. The co-operative itself owns the housing and each member has a share in the project. None of the units in such a co-operative can be sold for a profit.
Up until 1973, although building co-operatives received some assistance, continuing co-operatives under group ownership had great difficulty getting recognition and acceptance under the act. One problem was that legislation did not provide for co-operatives to obtain loans for low rental hous-
Housing
ing, except as the sponsor for a project in which residents did not have to be members. In other words, low income people could have housing provided for them but they could not own it through a co-operative.
Another problem was that co-operatives could obtain funding only for new projects, not for existing housing, nor even for the rehabilitation of existing housing. As a result, people in a rental project could not get an NHA loan to buy it co-operatively even if the landlord wished to sell it to them. This made it difficult to mount a strong national program of co-operative housing.
In 1973, however, new housing legislation helped co-operatives to develop fully as another housing alternative for low income Canadians. The two most important provisions in the new legislation at that time were first, that housing co-operatives could qualify for 100 per cent loans for non-profit, low rental housing; and, secondly, loans would be available for both the purchase and rehabilitation of existing housing. That new legislation did, in effect, start a new form of co-operative, one in which the members are collectively owners but individually are in a leasehold position. On one hand they have the proprietary rights of a landlord, and on the other hand the rights and advantages of tenants.
As the Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has mentioned, extensive discussions recently between his ministry and the co-operative Housing Foundation of Canada have produced an agreement regarding the administration of subsidies and charges to occupants of housing units that serve mutual objectives. The new agreement provides for fewer controls by CMHC on actual project development, and allows co-operatives to have the opportunity to use a wider range of procurement techniques based on the group's experience. Greater latitude is also given to co-operative groups in choosing between the acquisition of existing developments and the construction of new projects. The agreement provides, as well, for a significant increase in federal financial support to co-operative projects, and continued application of the residential rehabilitation assistance program.
There is no doubt that the new program will result in much higher production of this much needed type of accommodation. Federal assistance will be almost doubled, and private lending institutions indicate their willingness to invest as much as $500 million during the next few years in support of co-operative housing. This means that the number of people living in co-operative housing could easily double in a few years, going from the present level of about 50,000 to more than 100,000.
I am pleased that the government is giving support to co-operative housing as another means of offering another choice of housing tenure to families of various incomes. The new program will assist members of the co-operative housing program to build even more housing that they can afford and of which they can be proud.

March 6, 1979
Housing
I am particularly pleased that this bill preserves and extends one of the most important housing measures ever put forward in Canada. I am referring to the residential rehabilitation assistance program-RRAP. Restrictions have been removed from this program and its benefits are no longer limited to housing in certain specially designated areas. With the passage of this legislation, all Canadians will become eligible for RRAP assistance, within the terms of the program, and I have no doubt that the funds available to support it will be applied to the most pressing needs, wherever they may occur in Canada.
It is not surprising that the RRAP program met with such an immediate and enthusiastic response from the people of Canada. Since the program was introduced in 1973, CMHC has been assisting in the rehabilitation of some 20,000 units per year. As the program is broadened and municipal officials become more familiar with its application, that annual rate will increase. The number of homes that can be rehabilitated in any year depends a lot upon the capacity of municipal organizations to manage and implement the program.
All of the demographic trends, economic projections, and our shifting social values suggest that rehabilitation is going to be a more significant activity for at least the rest of this century. The government, in bringing forth these amendments, recognizing the importance of rehabilitation and conservation, has reaffirmed its intention to continue to support it in a tangible way.
I have a few comments concerning the deductibility of mortgage interest, Mr. Speaker. The Tory mortgage interest tax proposal is unjust and unnecessary. Furthermore, the taxpayer cannot afford it.
I should like to put some relevant statistics on the record which show that 62 per cent of Canadian families, some 4.4 million, are home owners while 38 per cent, or 2.4 million, rent their homes.
I should like for a moment to comment on living styles. In Quebec, 50 per cent of the people are home owners compared to 66 per cent in Ontario, 65 per cent in Alberta and 69 per cent in British Columbia. Francophones are only approximately 45 per cent home owners by living style, 55 per cent living in rented accommodation.
I stress this point, Mr. Speaker, because the Tory program makes no attempt to recognize the difference in living styles between Canadians in the province of Quebec and Canadians in the wealthier provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. The program is designed to aid to a much greater degree persons living in those two wealthier provinces of Alberta and British Columbia.
You will swallow anything.

speechtext:
Among home owners, 35 per cent have incomes below $10,000, 45 per cent between $10,000 and $20,000 and the rest earn over $20,000. Because marginal rates increase with income, the higher income earner benefits more. The 35 per cent of home owners who have a family income under $10,000 pay about 14 per cent of the total mortgage interest payments whereas the 20 per cent with incomes over $20,000 pay 33 per cent of the total mortgage interest payments.
High income earners are in a better position to borrow and these persons, together with those with debt-free homes choosing to benefit from the program, would receive preference from lending institutions. Lower income groups would face increased difficulty in securing funds.
In Quebec, the average family income for home owners is $19,300 whereas the average in Ontario is $22,500, in Alberta, $21,200 and in British Columbia $22,100. Thus, the marginal rate is higher in the wealthier provinces.
Lost revenues to the federal government would also entail losses to the provinces as fewer funds would be available for transfer. The provinces would have to raise taxes in order to replace these losses.
The amount of the downpayment is often the major problem for young couples wishing to buy houses. The increase in demand for mortgage money by those refinancing their homes with new or increased mortgages would tend to raise the amount of the downpayment required.
Those who have saved to increase the equity in their homes, either by increasing the downpayment or paying off part of the mortgage, will receive less benefit than those who have the minimum investment in their homes.
Tenants who choose not to buy a house or tenants who cannot buy a home would be obligated as taxpayers to contribute to the cost of a plan in which they do not choose to participate or are unable to participate.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO DEPRIVE CONVICTED WAR CRIMINALS OF CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
that Bill C-215, respecting war criminals in Canada, be read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on December 31, 1979, which is the end of this year, unless the German government acts to change its law, the statute of limitations in Germany will bar any further prosecution of Nazi war criminals. In that country the statute of limitations has been extended once already in connection with the commission of war crimes. In the public debate that was held in the German parliament I understand there was a mixed feeling and there is only a slight majority in favour of the further extension of the statute of limitations for war crimes.
The United States congress and some other national governments and legislatures around the world have unanimously passed resolutions urging the German government to extend its statute of limitations. I hope that at some early date this parliament will act similarly and pass a resolution by unani-
War Criminals
mous consent along the lines of those passed by others urging the Germans to extend their statute of limitations. If no action is taken by Germany we may then face the appalling spectacle of persons coming forward to publish and to sell memoirs of their World War II war crime commissions. Judging by the success of other books written by other sorts of criminals, we can anticipate that these books will make a lot of money for their authors. I very much regret to note that according to the record, a well established record, some of these books about war crimes could be written by Canadian citizens.
World War II was a trauma in history which we must seek to keep alive in everyone's memory. There are lessons to be learned from it about the values of democracy and society, and as well about the dangers of fascism and racism. These are lessons too important to be forgotten and yet too easily forgotten. Already there are those who seek to write this history for their own purposes. One needs to go no further than to give as an example the statement of a candidate in a recent federal by-election by the name of Roger Delorme, who denied that six million Jews, as well as many others, were murdered during World War II, and who claimed that the number was less than one million. I believe that we should fight against this re-writing of history. We must not forget. Canada has too much of a stake in World War II history. There were too many lives lost to allow what happened at that time to be forgotten.
What can we do to help keep intact our history of that war? One thing is to prosecute war criminals who are living in this country. I am proposing in this bill that if these people are prosecuted and convicted, their Canadian citizenship will be taken from them. It is clear that we have the jurisdiction to prosecute people guilty of war crimes here in Canada, even though the crimes may have been committed elsewhere in the world. We are signatories to the Geneva Conventions Act and there are precedents, five cases that I know of, in which Canadian courts prosecuted persons for committing war crimes that occurred in Europe. Our courts have already been prepared to assume jurisdiction in cases of war crimes.
My bill attempts a measure of justice to the memory of World War II. Millions of people have come to Canada who were victims of that war. These people have come from Europe as well as from other parts of the world. They have come looking for the opportunity to establish a better life. In most cases they have become citizens pursuant to the laws that were established by this parliament. Under our laws citizenship has always been discretionary, in the sense that there are tests to be met and criteria applied. But above and beyond these things the government has had the discretion to withhold citizenship in appropriate cases.
I understand that for a fairly long period in our recent history we inquired into communist affiliations and activity by would-be Canadian citizens. If we were satisfied that they were members of a communist or fascist government or had close ties with one, we took steps to withhold Canadian citizenship from them. I understand also that in some cases, by misrepresentation in citizenship applications, citizenship was wrongly obtained by some individuals.
3874

March 6, 1979
War Criminals
There are safeguards provided in the Citizenship Act. There is a procedure provided whereby an individual who obtains Canadian citizenship by false representation or fraud can have his Canadian citizenship revoked. To my knowledge we fail to press the matter of war crimes as diligently as we pressed the matter of communist affiliation. We did not press the question: Was the individual involved in the commission of war crimes? Opinions have been given that those who have obtained Canadian citizenship and were guilty of war crimes but who represented otherwise may well be entitled to keep Canadian citizenship.
There are, of course, other legal opinions. In the preparation of my brief remarks today I read a legal opinion setting out grounds under which Canadian citizenship might be revoked. These grounds were non-disclosure of the commission of war crimes. Unless we take some positive action and amend our legislation we will have no recourse against these individuals.
Hon. members may ask who I am talking about. I do not intend to name names in this chamber. However, it is well known that there are over one dozen individuals in this category in Canada. Witnesses are available from among the Ukrainian and Jewish population who have come from Europe who can give evidence against these individuals. In my opinion they ought to do so and may do so if the provision such as the one I am proposing is introduced.
I have been somewhat vague in my reference to the term "war criminals" and to its definition. I have not used the term "war criminals" in my bill. The term used is "an offence pursuant to section 3 of the Geneva Conventions Act". That refers to grave breaches which include, among other things, wilful killing, torture or inhuman treatment, including biological experiments, and wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health. I am ascerting that it is well known that there are people in Canada who come within that definition by virtue of their conduct. I am suggesting that action ought to be taken against them and the bill which I have proposed, if enacted, will make it easier and more likely to do so.
I want to add one other matter which I have covered in this bill. In my opinion, it is not fair that the bill be restricted in its effect only to those who have acquired Canadian citizenship by naturalization and not to those Canadian born. I am not proposing that any distinction be drawn. It is conceivable that a born Canadian was in Europe or in another theatre of war and committed a crime within the definition I have put forward. The bill provides that his citizenship also is subject to revocation, not only the citizenship of an immigrant. I am not in favour of making any more differences between Canadians who have acquired their citizenship by birth and those who have acquired their citizenship by naturalization. If implemented, this bill will operate equally against both, whether naturalized or born in Canada.
This provision is not limited only to World War II. God knows, we have evidence of the commission of war crimes in

all wars. The amendment I am suggesting here would be applicable to those circumstances as well. It is by no means limited, although I began my remarks talking about the World War II experience and the holocaust.
This is a simple bill. It is easy to understand. It is timely because of what is now happening in Germany. It can be taken as an example and demonstration of the strong feelings Canadians have that we not forget what happened in World War II, and that we not allow those who were responsible for serious crimes during that war to go unpunished. Canadian citizenship should not continue to be held by those who are guilty of war crimes.
I look forward to learning whether the government favours or does not favour the principle of the bill. Whether it does or not, I hope that my colleagues on all sides of the House will make it possible for this important measure to be referred to the justice committee so that evidence can be led on its effect and the need for it. Because I assert that this is a bill that is needed and is needed now.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO DEPRIVE CONVICTED WAR CRIMINALS OF CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) for bringing this matter forward for discussion in the House this afternoon. I agree with many of the sentiments he expressed, but I do not agree with the vehicle of Bill C-215. It proposes to take a very drastic course on the part of the Government of Canada. I hope to develop arguments in the next few minutes as to why it should not be pursued.
The subject matter is important. Because of the remarks made by my colleague from York Centre I personally would agree to having the subject matter referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
I agree with my colleague that the Government of Canada should urge the West German government to extend its statute of limitations for prosecution of war crimes. I understand it will run out later this year. The magnitude of the atrocities in the Second World War by war crime elements is such that this statute of limitations should be allowed to be extended so that justice may pursue many of those who have eluded authority since the Second World War. In that sense I fully support the hon. member for York Centre.
I also support his general premise that today, almost 35 years after the end of the Second World War, we should not allow the lessons learned in that war to be forgotten. I grew up in post-war England, in central London, where the effects of the war were very apparent upon families which lost many lives in the bombing and went to school with kids whose fathers did not come home.
The war had a very profound effect on me even though I was born a year after it ended. It is something that will stay with me for the rest of my life. One of the most moving days in the year, even before I became a politician, was November 11 and our Remembrance Day ceremonies. We of all generations must do our utmost to ensure that the lessons of the Second World War do not go unheeded for future generations. In that
March 6, 1979

sense I fully support the hon. member for York Centre and his intentions.
The bill as projected by the hon. member would place severe constraints upon Canadian law. I wish to develop these arguments now. The bill proposes that the Citizenship Act be amended so that any Canadian citizen convicted of war crimes in World War II should automatically cease to be a Canadian. The hon. member did not use those words, but that is what would happen. He talked in terms of section 9(1) being amended by the following words:
Notwithstanding any other Act, every person convicted of an offence pursuant to section 3 of the Geneva Conventions Act thereby ceases to be a Canadian citizen.
Its effect is to amend the Citizenship Act so that any Canadian citizen convicted of war crimes in the Second World War should automatically cease to be a Canadian. What the amendment seeks to do is entirely outside the philosophy of the Citizenship Act and the very liberal approach taken in this country towards citizenship, especially in the last few years, but historically. In that sense the hon. member for York Centre has good intentions but is somewhat misguided in the remedy he seeks to place before the House.
The Citizenship Act of February 15, 1977 is unique in the world. I wish to quote the former secretary of state, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner), when speaking on February 24, 1976. He said:
What makes this bill unique and a leader among nationality laws of the world? ... it treats absolutely everyone equally... This quality is rare in citizenship law. But,... the new Citizenship Act... clearly lays down certain steps the applicant must follow and certain qualifications the applicant must satisfy. Upon satisfaction of those conditions, then citizenship shall follow as a right.
In other words, the Citizenship Act recognizes that a person has a right to be a citizen of Canada after he or she has met the requirements set forth in the Citizenship Act and has completed the application procedures, including a person to person interview with a citizenship judge and the taking of the oath of citizenship in court. Not only is the Citizenship Act designed to be equitable in the acquisition of citizenship but also in the loss of it. That is an essential point to remember; equity in acceptance and equity in terms of losing citizenship. Already, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you can see how anomalous the amendment proposed in Bill C-215 would be in the Citizenship Act. We must, however, press on to other facts.
Citizenship may be revoked if, after being lawfully admitted to Canada, it is proven that the person entered Canada by false representation, fraud, or by concealing material circumstances or by obtaining citizenship by the same means. My colleague acknowledges that point. The governor in council, upon a report from the Secretary of State, has had to revoke citizenship from time to time. However, in order to do so, it must have been able positively to identify individuals in the records of citizenship registration which have been kept since 1868. To date, the citizenship branch has been unable to identify individuals alleged to be war criminals since, in all probability, most would have changed their identity before entering Canada. How then, would the branch be in any better
War Criminals
position to identify individuals in its records for the purpose of Bill C-215?
It must also be borne in mind that under the Citizenship Act the citizen may request that, before the minister makes a report to the governor in council requesting revocation of his citizenship, his case be referred to the trial division of the Federal Court of Canada. But Bill C-215, if passed, would mean that individuals convicted under section 3 of the Geneva Convention Act, 1965, would have no recourse in law to plead that their citizenship should not be revoked, and would be at an extreme disadvantage vis-a-vis other Canadian citizens. Here we see the essential liberal philosophy which has underlined our legal sense since 1867 being skirted. At one stroke, Canadians affected by Bill C-215 would be stripped of their equality before the law and the their right to Canadian citizenship.
To introduce this automatic loss provision would remove the right of some Canadians either to voluntarily relinquish citizenship or to state their case before the Federal Court. Above all, adoption of Bill C-215 would make a partial, if not total, mockery of Canada's Human Rights Act. I am sure the hon. member for York Centre, who is an ardent proponent of human rights and a strong supporter of the human rights legislation passed by this parliament, would not want his bill to contravene the spirit of the Human Rights Act.
Another factor which must be considered is that both the Geneva conventions of 1948 and 1965 and the Canadian act respecting Geneva conventions for the protection of war victims are not retroactive to 1939. Their intent is to prevent the kinds of crime which led up to Nuremberg. The intent of Bill C-215 is, of course, to strike off the register of Canadian citizens all who are convicted of war crimes in the 1939-1945 conflict in Nazi-occupied territory. Under the Citizenship Act, the judge is precluded from questioning applicants on their activity prior to entry to Canada, including war activity. The citizenship judge may consider only criminal activity which has occurred in Canada within the three years immediately preceding the date of the application. This provision in the Citizenship Act, therefore, renders the amendment useless in practice.
As well as being in contravention of our Human Rights Act and diametrically opposed to the spririt and intent of the Citizenship Act, the implementation of Bill C-215 could create stateless persons. Particularly liable to this fate would be the former nationals or citizens of countries which no longer exist. In addition, it could affect persons born in Canada who have no other nationality. Canada, again in the spirit of human rights, signed on October 15, 1978, the United Nations convention on the reduction of statelessness. Canada has thus pledged to presume that every person is entitled to a nationality regardless of any crimes he or she may have committted.
A couple of months ago the whole concept of citizenship was brought up by the return to Canada of FLQ members involved in certain events in Quebec in the early 1970s. In particular,

March 6, 1979
War Criminals
the Cossette-Trudels came here. I know their case is before the courts and I do not want to reflect upon their guilt or innocence, but these people have been charged by the Crown with committing certain criminal acts and they will be brought to trial. Many people in my constituency had an instant reaction along these lines: why would we want these people back in Canada; why not leave them in France or in Cuba? Of course, these people were prejudging guilt, but the essence of this issue is that, notwithstanding any crimes which the accused may have committed, they did not revoke their citizenship upon leaving Canada. I do not know whether this was a specific intent of the minister of justice at the time or whether it was stipulated as part of the arrangement when these people went into exile, when they were given free passage to leave Canada, but it was always understood that the Crown alleged they had committed certain crimes and should they come back to Canada the accused would have to face justice.
I can defend the right of these people to return to this country as a right to face the Canadian justice system. It is important when we talk about revoking the right of citizenship that we keep in mind Canada's commitment to the United Nations and our pledge that every person is entitled to nationality irrespective of any crimes or misdemeanours that he or she might have engaged in. Canada has agreed to uphold article 8(1) of the convention, which states:
A contracting state shall not deprive a person of its nationality if such deprivation would render him stateless.
In certain circumstances, such as treason, the convention permits the contracting state to deprive a person of citizenship, even though the person would then become stateless. Even then, though, the convention rules that the deprivation must be in accordance with the law "which shall provide for the person concerned the right to a fair hearing by a court or other independent body". But Bill C-215 provides for automatic loss of citizenship in contravention of the convention on the reduction of statelessness.
Just suppose, in spite of all the arguments we have presented, the bill passes and the stateless person, or national of some other country, is extradited. Where shall the person go? To a communist bloc country with whom Canada has no extradition treaty? To a country which no longer exists?
Mr. Speaker, the adoption of Bill C-215 would be in direct conflict with the spirit and intent of the Citizenship Act. Furthermore, it contravenes what Canada has already agreed to, the provisions of the convention on the reduction of statelessness. For these reasons, I oppose the bill.
Nevertheless, for the reasons which I outlined earlier, I believe this whole subject of lessons to be learned from the holocaust, the crimes committed in the Second World War, the pursuit of war criminals and the importance of West Germany continuing its statute of limitations, should lead us to think that this would be a very good subject matter for reference to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and I will certainly support such a move if it is agreeable to hon. members.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude-Andre Lachance (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO DEPRIVE CONVICTED WAR CRIMINALS OF CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the preceding speaker, and in spite of the reservations I have about it and on which I shall elaborate later, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) for sponsoring this bill. This bill is indeed inspired by a commendable ideal and, like the preceding speaker, I am convinced that the House will probably feel the need one day to draw lessons from history and do its utmost to prevent the reoccurence of misfortunes such as those which happened at the time.
To come to grasps, since we must, with the contents of Bill C-215, an act respecting war criminals in Canada, I would like, if I may, Mr. Speaker, to examine with the House some of the implications the implementation of this bill would have both domestically and for our commitments to the international community.
Bill C-215 would add new section 9.1 immediately after section 9 of the Citizenship Act found in the Statutes of Canada 1974-75-76, chapter 108. The new section would provide that any person convicted of an offence pursuant to section 3 of the Geneva Conventions Act, chapter G-3 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1970, would thereby cease to be a Canadian citizen.
What are these Geneva conventions? It might be a good idea to find out what we are talking about. The above-mentioned act approves the four Geneva conventions on the protection of war victims signed in Geneva on August 12, 1949. These four conventions are: first, the convention for the relief of the wounded and sick in armies in the field; second, the convention for the amelioration of the condition of the wounded, sick and the shipwrecked members of armed forces at sea; third, the convention on the treatment of war prisoners; finally, four, the convention on the protection of civilian persons in time of war.
Section 3 of the act stipulates that any "grave breach" of any of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, as therein defined, that would, if committed in Canada, be an offence under any provision of the Criminal Code or other act of the Parliament of Canada, is an offence under such provision of the Criminal Code or other act if committed outside Canada. "Grave breach" is defined in the four conventions as follows: first, in that on the armed forces in the field, at article 50; second, in that on the armed forces at sea, at article 51; third, in that on the prisoners of war, at article 130; and four, in that on civilian persons, at article 147.
Grave breaches include the following crimes which are committed on persons or property protected by the Conventions, namely, wilful killing, torture or inhuman treatment, including biological experiments, and wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health; the massive
March 6, 1979

destruction and appropriation of property unless it is justified by military imperatives and made legally and wisely.
Section 3 grants extra-territorial jurisdiction to Canadian courts with regard to crimes committed outside Canada when they fall within the limits set forth in the four conventions mentioned earlier. Those crimes fall within the jurisdiction of the court where the accused is located, and that is where he will be judged and punished if proved guilty. Still, the attorney general must given his consent in writing before legal procedures can get under way.
What would be the effect of the implementation of Bill C-215 within the territorial limits of Canada? My colleague, the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette), enumerated a while ago some of the legal consequences under the Citizenship Act; I should like to come back to that because it strikes me as being fundamental.
The Citizenship Act of 1976, which replaced that of 1970 found in chapter 19 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1970, makes it easier to acquire the Canadian citizenship and keep it. It is the right of those who are protected by the act, and can only be lost or withdrawn under the terms of the second part of the act. And there are three ways to lose Canadian citizenship: first, by renunciation as provided in section 8; second, by order of the governor in council, where the citizenship was obtained by fraud or by knowingly concealing material circumstances as provided in section 9; and third, by the fact, for a person who was born in a country other than Canada from at least one Canadian parent, of not having asked to retain his Canadian citizenship or nor having registered and gone to live in Canada during at least one year before the age of 28, as provided in section 7.
The deprivation of citizenship because of conviction for a criminal offence is inconsistent with the spirit of the act which reduced the number of reasons justifying the deprivation of citizenship. Such deprivation can be an extreme punishment by making the person concerned stateless, and I shall come back on this matter a little later. This is what would happen to the person born in Canada without having another citizenship or to the person born outside Canada who would have lost his or her original citizenship by becoming a Canadian citizen.
Although it looks simplistic, that bill would have very serious effects as regards the international commitments we freely agreed to make. The nationality which encompasses citizenship is an important factor in international law because it is the very basis of the international protection granted by a state to one of its citizens. Furthermore, diplomatic immunity abroad is also based on the nationality.
The United Nations took an active part in establishing everyone's right to a nationality. On December 10, 1948, the General Assembly, then made up of 58 countries, adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Forty-eight countries voted for it, eight abstained and two were not represented.
War Criminals
None voted against it. Here is what article 15 of the declaration says, and I quote:
(1)	Everyone has the right to a nationality;
(2)	No one shall be arbitrarily deprived of his nationality nor denied the right to change his nationality.
As the declaration is not a treaty, there was no need to have it signed or ratified. However, it remains a statement of principle of the highest moral authority. Called the Great Charter, it spells out a common objective for all countries and nations and as far as I know Canada endorses these objectives.
Moreover, and to be more specific, certain international conventions emanating from the United Nations deal with nationality in a very specific way. The convention relating to the status of stateless persons adopted on September 28, 1954 and in force since June 6, 1960, to which Canada is not party, provides the following in article 32 entitled Naturalization:
The contracting states shall, inasmuch as possible, facilitate the assimilation and the naturalization of stateless persons. They shall endeavour in particular to accelerate the naturalization process and to reduce inasmuch as possible the fees and costs involved.
On the other hand, the convention on the reduction of statelessness adopted on August 30, 1961, in force since December 13, 1975 and ratified by Canada on October 15, 1978, provides the following in article 8(1):
The contracting states shall not deprive any individual from his nationality were that deprivation to make him stateless.
The mover clearly stated his intention not to make any distinction between withdrawal of nationality from people who have had another nationality in the past and who have settled in Canada and Canadians who were born in Canada and who would be submitted to the same arbitrary judgment. Obviously, in the second case, this approach would directly result in making these people stateless persons.
That obligation, as stipulated in article 8 of the convention on the reduction of statelessness, is ineffective, however, when the nationality has been obtained by means of a false statement or any other fraudulent act or when the individual has resided in a foreign country for a period of time not inferior to seven consecutive years without informing the proper authorities of his intention to retain his nationality or when the individual has allowed one full year to elapse from the date of his majority without establishing a residence on the territory of the state or without registering with the proper authorities of that state.
There again, Mr. Speaker, there is no mention about the problem of Canadians born in Canada who would be arbitrarily deprived of their nationality.
The International Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Racial Discrimination, adopted on December 21, 1965, in force since January 4, 1969 and ratified by Canada on October 14, 1970, stipulates, at section 5(d) (iii), and I quote:

March 6, 1979
War Criminals
Pursuant to the fundamental obligations set out in section 2 of this Convention, the Member States agree to prohibit and eliminate all forms of racial discrimination and guarantee to everyone the right to equality before the law regardless of race, colour, or national or ethnic origin, especially for the enjoyment of the following rights:
In particular, subsection (d):
(d) Other civil rights, especially:
In particular, also, paragraph (iii)
(iii) The right to a nationality;
One can therefore see in this section a direct cause and effect relationship between nationality and discrimination.
Revocation of citizenship on the grounds of conviction for an offense is incompatible with the spirit of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, as we have seen, and is a direct breach by Canada of its international commitments pursuant to the Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. Even when it is not on racial grounds, revocation of citizenship is a direct breach of the spirit embodied in the International Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Racial Discrimination.
Also, such a revocation would go against the United Nations' efforts to improve the quality of life for stateless persons. It is therefore obvious, Mr. Speaker, that on an international level, Bill C-215 would have major negative effects and would force Canada to renege on commitments it freely agreed to by ratifying certain treaties, in particular those I referred to.
Finally, the third negative effect that I see in the implementation of Bill C-215, if it was passed in its present form, concerns criminal law. The revocation of the citizenship of a person convicted of grave breach of one of the articles of the Geneva convention would result in a different treatment, depending whether such person had committed his or her crime in Canada or elsewhere. This would result in a further punishment for the person who had acted outside Canada. This situation would be inconsistent with the Latin maxim nemo debet bis puniri pro uno delicto; in other words, no one should be liable to be punished more than once for the same offence. This same maxim is expressed differently in section 11 of the Criminal Code.
The revocation of citizenship is therefore foreign to our Criminal Code where a convicted person may be either imprisoned, fined or given a suspended sentence with a recommendation for probation. But nowhere is there mention of revocation of citizenship. It could be argued that such a penalty would impose a cruel and unusual punishment, in violation of section 2(b) of our Bill of rights which is found in the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1970.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the principle of this bill or at least its intent is contrary to the Canadian policies in the area of citizenship and criminal law, as well as our international commitments. However, I would like to reconsider the fact

that there is now a popular movement for the remembrance of what happened in the Second World War. I was not then a politician but I am conscious of course of the entirely negative impact of that war and more especially for those who experienced harsh treatment in the hands of Nazi authorities.
The whole debate dealing with the statute of limitation in Germany must necessarily be carefully followed here. This is why in spite of my serious reservations about the mechanism of Bill C-215, which if it was passed in its present form, would compel Canada to review some agreements at the international level and on the other hand, to review some basic principles, more especially the principle stating that one cannot be condemned twice for the same crime and other legislation, more particularly the immigration legislation which does not provide for such penalty and finally would compel parliament to review its basic philosophy underlying the comprehension citizenship issue, one of the most liberal with a small "1" in the world even if I have very serious reservations, I still think that because of the concern of the member and of other Canadians toward this matter of the war criminals and the fact that the memory of the atrocities committed during World War II that must be kept alive, as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) I would accept, Mr. Speaker, that a motion be presented so that this bill be withdrawn and its subject matter referred to the committee on justice and legal affairs so that the members of that committee may discuss together means and mechanisms which would enable us to see to it that the lesson of the Second World War be well remembered by Canadians and that we may try to find means to avoid that these horrors be repeated once again.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part in this debate, and I begin by reiterating some of the comments of the previous speaker, the hon. member for Lafon-taine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance). I should like to remind hon. members and Canadians of the awful experience humanity has faced in the last 50 years. Also, it is good to remind people of what took place between 1939 and 1945. The abuse and cruelty some people were subjected to during those difficult years are fresh in the minds of those who participated in that conflict.
I will not deal with the legal aspect of Bill C-215 as some of my colleagues have done so already, but I should like to add another dimension in the first few words of my contribution. [Translation]
The tragedies which mankind experienced all too often, Mr. Speaker, are still too fresh in the memory of a great many Canadians. However, for those of our fellow citizens who have not experienced what is a total war such as that of 1939-45, such a concept is so remote from the mind of these people that they find it difficult to truly perceive what these people who have lived through the war have endured, be they those people
March 6, 1979

who lived on the continent or in England, our enemies or our allies. It is an experience, Mr. Speaker, which left a mark on all of us who have contributed in some manner or who have actually participated in that conflict and it is a story which should be regularly reminded, as I mentioned earlier, so that no one may forget the memory of these trying times humanity went through.
As French-speaking Canadians from the province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker, when reference is made to Canadian citizenship we ascribe, or at least I do, a great value to a citizenship which we hold so dear to our hearts.
The purpose of this bill is to take away from the known war criminals this great privilege of going about freely posing as Canadians and enjoying Canadian citizenship. Mr. Speaker, war criminals, those who have been found or who will be found guilty of war crimes against whichever nationality, and incidentally, some 15 of them are said to live in Canada, should be denounced, they should be stripped of their Canadian citizenship so that mankind may know that once and for all there is no longer any room in this modern world for this kind of abuse, such atrocities and acts of violence.
This is even more important, Mr. Speaker, when we consider the situation throughout the world and the great temptation that certain politicians have to use violence occasionally to get what they want. In view of what goes on at the present time and since I have seen this much more directly, Mr. Speaker, for having passed the three months of the Third Assembly of the United Nations in New York, I was able to see and hear every day reports of serious incidents involving violence where people have lost their lives or been tortured in certain countries to meet the objectives of others.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, will help warn everyone, and especially those who would be tempted to use violence to serve their own interests, that you must always be ready to face the consequences of your actions. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that Germany and the German people will have no objection if their compatriots who brought so much shame on the noble German people are denounced and have to pay for their crimes.
It seems that two or three other countries have passed similar legislation to ensure that all those who are found guilty of crimes against the Jews will be punished fairly and according to the best legal practices. As I say, two or three countries have already passed similar legislation to ensure that those who fled Germany at the last minute to avoid being held responsible for their actions will be prosecuted and will serve their sentences.
Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that my interest in this legislation lies mostly in wanting to ensure that everyone will remember the terrible ills of war and the hardship that certain races or nations faced because of these conflicts. What is most important, Mr. Speaker, is that this legislation will remind us that we are always responsible for our actions and that those
War Criminals
who have not yet been prosecuted should be as soon as possible. I understand that another of my colleagues would like to contribute to this debate, Mr. Speaker, and I thank you for the time which was allotted to me.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to become involved in this matter only briefly. The hon. member who introduced the bill made the point at the beginning of discussing statutory limitation, saying that statutory limitation for murder has been discussed with increasing frequency in this and other countries of the world. In other western countries almost the only question is whether murders committed during the Nazi era come under the statute of limitations. The federal government of Germany, in my opinion, has so far failed to put before the public in Canada and in other countries the facts about this particular matter.
Since in Britain and in the United States, in particular, the statute of limitations, is for the most part an unknown facet of the law, many people tend to see the expiry of that period as a general amnesty. Hardly anybody in these countries is aware that currently over 3,000 cases involving probable Nazi crimes are the subject of legal proceedings of one form or another in West Germany, and that about 4,000 cases involving investigatory proceedings are to be completed by the year 2000. Nor have Canadians and Americans been made aware of the fact that in the ten years since 1969, when the period of statutory limitation was extended from 20 to 30 years, only three offenders have been convicted. Some of the condemnation then of the Federal Republic of Germany and its statute of limitations that we hear in the west would not have been forthcoming if the federal government of Germany had done its duty and saw to it that the necessary information was made available.
I make that point particularly when our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been such a close friend of the Chancellor of Germany over the past few years, during which time, at meetings between the Prime Minister and Mr. Schmidt, the points raised this afternoon in the hon. member's bill must have been mentioned.
In the meantime, the chairman of the SPD parliamentary party, the party that has formed the government in Germany, has also joined in the debate. This man, with his attitude at a time when Stalin was committing wholesale murder, can hardly have a claim to be heard on this of all problems. He calls MPs in Germany not in favour of dispensing with the statute of limitations "injudicious". His intervention has poisoned the opinion of parliamentary parties, and the leaders of the government cannot seem to make him stop these comments which have made it, frankly, doubtful, as the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) says, whether a majority can be mustered to scrap the statute of limitations.
As a member of the official opposition, in lending some support to the hon. member for York Centre I should like to point out that I have colleagues in West Germany in a similar

March 6, 1979
War Criminals
minded party who are included to favour the abolition of the statute of limitations, but they see themselves in the company of a man whose own standards have been called into question, which indeed prejudices their position in the matter.
I thought that in these few moments I should make the point that in fact the socialist government in Germany has not taken the steps it should and could have taken, to make this matter so much more clear cut and, therefore, make it so much easier to adopt abolition completely, which would have overcome the necessity for a bill such as the one introduced by the hon. member for York Centre. I understand that, for a change, the hon. member for York Centre has induced his government colleagues to allow the content of the bill to go to the committee. It might appear I am standing here with the possibility of talking it out, but I assure you that I have given my word to the hon. member that I will not do that. I will now sit down and allow the bill to go to the committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was interrupted by the clock at 5 p.m. I was talking about the Tory program of mortgage interest deductibility and I was listing some points I considered that should be brought to the attention of the population of Canada. If these points were better understood by Canadians, it might eliminate some of the popularity of this program which exists at the present time.
I had outlined several items, and it is from that point I would like to continue. For example, I turn now to the problem senior citizens will encounter with the Tory scheme. I am speaking of those senior citizens who own their own homes and have long since paid off their mortgages. Because of their age, and despite their equity positions, they will find that lending institutions will be unwilling to provide funds that would enable them to take advantage of the tax benefits in the scheme. It is well known that lending institutions are often reluctant to lend moneys to elderly people for home mortgages.
March 6, 1979

Those who have small mortgages or no mortgages at all will find themselves in the impossible position of not being able to borrow funds in order to take advantage of the Tory deductibility plan. People who can afford to increase their mortgages can use the moneys raised for other purposes, that is, to buy goods or pleasures. They can do this at the expense of the taxpayers generally, many of whom cannot afford a home and certainly cannot afford the extras that will be bought with the tax subsidized proceeds. If a person with little or no mortgage wants to take a trip around the world, that person can very easily increase his mortgage or take out a mortgage on his home and use these funds for whatever purpose he wants, perhaps to purchase a car or to finance a trip. This person can then deduct the interest on these borrowed funds and gain the benefits from the Tory plan.
Home building of the kind that would benefit from this program has always been strong. A look at the statistics would indicate that in the case of single family residences there has been no fall off in construction of this type of house in Canada, with the exception of the province of Quebec. In that province the fall off has been fairly appreciable because of political reasons. The strength in the building of this type of home would illustrate that this is not the kind of construction that needs further boosting.
The United States permits mortgage interest deductibility. A comparison with the United States shows that Canada's record of home building, on a per capita basis, is and always has been vastly superior to that in the United States. At this point I would like to cite some figures. In the ten-year period from 1967 to 1976 one can see that whilst the high in 1972 in the U.S. was some 2,379,000 homes built, the low in 1975 was 1,171,000 homes, and the average is somewhere about 1.5 million homes built per annum. In Canada for the same period the high recorded in 1976 was 273,203 homes built, and the low was 190,528 homes built in 1970, giving an average of approximately 250,000 homes built per annum. This would indicate on a rough ten for one basis-the population of the United States being approximately ten times that of the population of Canada-that home building in Canada has been substantially stronger than home building in the United States. In fact, home building in Canada on a per capita basis has been in the order of 60 per cent higher than that in the United States.
The Carter Royal Commission on Taxation said that the tax system should avoid tax concessions to particular kinds of income, that such tax concessions are always inequitable. I suggest that the Tory proposition is about as inequitable a tax system as they could come up with. Since we have been talking of comparisons between Canada and the United States, I should mention that profit on the sale of a house in Canada is free of capital gains tax. This is not so in the United States. This Tory program will probably cause some major disruptions in the financial market, especially in its initial stages.
There is one other point I wish to mention in the remaining time I have. It deals with the Tory allegations of excessive defaults in the Assisted Home Ownership Program. AHOP
Housing
loans in arrears do not automatically constitute a default. As of December last year only 1.62 per cent of direct AHOP loans administered by CMHC were in arrears three months or more. One year previously the rate was 1.31 per cent. One can translate that into percentages and come up with a fairly large increase. I would guess it would amount to something in the order of 20 per cent or 25 per cent. However, the default rate is still 1.31 per cent.
The percentage for all NHA insured loans in arrears three months or more as of December 31, 1978, was 0.99 per cent, that is, less than 1 per cent. The Conservatives are making a lot of noise about this because they are able to apply the percentage of AHOP defaults against the percentage of regular defaults. If we look at the figures we will see that very little of the moneys which have been put into the insurance of mortgages has been used. In other words, the losses have been almost negligible.
The application of a percentage to AHOP defaults against regular NHA insured loan defaults will give an obviously false impression. I would suggest it would be a good thing if we used some of the large fund which has been built up from insurance moneys received by CMHC to ensure the construction of additional homes for people with low incomes.
In closing may I reiterate a point which I think is most important. As I said earlier, the average income in Quebec is $19,300 per annum for home owners compared to a figure of $22,500 in Ontario, $21,200 in Alberta, and $22,100 in British Columbia, meaning that the Albertan home owner's income is $2,000 more than that of the Quebecker, and in Ontario and British Columbia approximately $3,000 more.
As I mentioned before, 33 per cent of total mortgage interest payments are paid by those with incomes over $20,000. Since Francophones in Quebec are only approximately 45 per cent home owners compared to 69 per cent in British Columbia, 66 per cent in Ontario and 65 per cent in Alberta, the discrimination between the wealthier provinces of Alberta and British Columbia compared to the people living in Quebec must be obvious to everyone.
As I suggested earlier, it is this discrimination that I find most unjust in the Tory proposal. I would like to hear from some of the Tories how they are going to account for this attitude toward the people of Quebec who have lower incomes and who do not have as many homes on a percentage basis as in English Canada. Because of their lower incomes they are paying lower rates of income tax. Therefore, their total benefit per capita is going to be substantially less than for those in Alberta and British Columbia, the two wealthier provinces in this country.
I am not speaking against the riches of the west of this country. It is good for our country as a whole. However, when we talk so often about what is going into the province of Quebec, I suggest that the Tory scheme is going in exactly the reverse direction. I would ask them sincerely to reconsider
