their attitude toward the Francophone home owner in the province of Quebec.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before I get into the main subject of my remarks on this legislation, I just want to refer to the parliamentary secretary's remarks which have obviously been prepared or certainly vetted by somebody in the department of urban affairs because they were pretty urbane.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I prepared my own remarks.

If the hon. member prepared his own remarks, they are still urbane. They are not germane. As far as AHOP is concerned, the best thing this government can do is AHOP to the polls because we are tired of waiting for that crowd to put their record on the line, instead of getting up in this House with all their dreary arguments against the mortgage deductibility scheme. To see you hon. gentlemen trying to crawl through the head of a pin, trying to argue against the mortgage interest deductibility, is really remarkable.
The hon. member now pretends it is a sinister scheme against the Francophones. What he won't stoop to in order to try to hold his seat in Quebec. That shows we are likely to get 60 seats. They are worried about their seats in Quebec. The hon. member says it is a sinister plot against the Francophones that we are going to make mortgage interest deductible. Have you ever in your life heard anything more ridiculous than that statement?
The parliamentary secretary got up and he started bleating about the fact that we had taken two weeks. He bleated piteously that we had taken two weeks to discuss housing amendments in this chamber. Two weeks is not long enough to discuss housing amendments if they are serious amendments. However, I discovered that the parliamentary secretary did not know what he was talking about. It was not a big discovery. I suspected it.
I had my researcher check the record. Here it is. We have not been ten days, eight days, six days or five days. We have been merely four days discussing housing amendments. Friday, February 23, two hours, 10 minutes, Monday, February 26, all day; Wednesday, February 28, 40 measly minutes; Thursday, March 1, all day; Friday, March 2, 20 minutes. The hon. gentleman did not want us to spend 20 minutes on it. Monday, March 5, all day, and today. To date we have had three days. If you take three parts of days it gets us up to four days of debate, not two weeks. If this government cannot stand having its legislation scrutinized in this chamber for four days, it should get out of office.
Where is the minister tonight, the minister who announced all these amendments six or eight months ago? The minister announced the amendments and he is not even here to listen to our comments and learn something. He is cowering somewhere. He is worried about the Francophones being attacked badly by a mortgage interest deductibility in Quebec. That is what he is doing.
Let me just say this. Methinks the hon. parliamentary secretary doth protest too much. What is so bad about mort-

gage interest deductibility that we cannot have it in Canada, that the fabric of our society and the Francophone element are going to be trampled underfoot and ruined altogether if we have mortgage interest deductibility up to an amount of $5,000 per year phased in over four years with $1,000 a year municipal taxes also made deductible?
The people in my district of St. John's West want it. Those who are not home owners are renters and they want it because they are going to become home owners. They are not worried about all of these things that the hon. gentleman points out. They know they have had it in the United States for years and the social fabric has not disintegrated in that country. They also know they have had it in other countries. Let us not hear any more of these piteous Liberal whines because they did not have the courage and the audacity to bring forward this imaginative tax reform themselves. This alone is enough to win me a huge majority in St. John's West. The more Liberals that come down there Fighting and attacking this, the better off we will be.
Have you ever seen a government with a majority that so mealy-mouthed its way around the House of Commons as this one? They cannot control the time of the House for some reason. It is the fault of the opposition that this bill does not come forward. It is the fault of the opposition if that bill does not come forward. It is the fault of the opposition if four days are spent on this. It is the fault of the opposition if two days are spent on that, or two weeks on something else.
Hear, hear!

What do they want? Do they want all 265 seats? Is that what they want? Well, sir, they are never going to get that. They may have come close to it in the past, but they have had it this time. I am going to leave the parliamentary secretary limp, dangling in defeat, with his 35 minutes forgotten about, because I demolished his whole argument in merely three or four minutes, and I will now come to this bill.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was once a fine institution, strong, a good housing agency. However, it has been molested. This government should be arrested for Central Mortgage molesting, just like the child molesters. It is this government that has molested CMHC. It has brought it from a high platform, from an institution that was respected till today, to the slingy, grey, dim stage that it is today, with scandal after scandal running across the country in CMHC offices, just like an attack of the measles across this country. That is what has happened by political interference by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, politically interfering and molesting CMHC. It has brought it to the position that everywhere you look there is a scandal. I am going to deal with one in my own constituency in a few minutes.
They have despoiled Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It used to be well thought of across the country, respected everywhere, but this political interference, this patronage fount, has turned it into a fount of patronage.

Prove it.
March 6, 1979

I will prove it; just wait a few minutes. The minister of state for graftology, I call him, the minister in charge of urban affairs. Now they are going to do away with urban affairs and molest it behind the scenes. They had been molesting it in public. Now they are going to do away with the department and do it quietly.
It's the ministry of state for poltroonery, Mr. Speaker, that's what it is. It's the ministry of state for political affairs. It's the ministry of state for "spoil the party friends." Every Liberal lawyer in the country has his tongue lapping out, hoping it will lap up some of those fees that they get, the legal fees and the emoluments that are given by the Liberal government which appoints them to act on CMHC mortgages.
I have given you this aphorism before, and I will repeat it: you might as well open an oyster without a knife as a lawyer's mouth without a fee. But I can tell the House that the Liberal lawyers of this country have got their mouths open. The oysters are all on this side. We cannot get a pea out of it. No way one looks at it, it is patronage gone putrid. It is dingy purse-cutting for political reasons. It is the ministry of state for purse-cutting that cut the purses out of the Canadian people in this institution. They have brought it down from a vibrant, dynamic, well-recognized, leading housing authority, to this slingy object that we see before us whenever we look at the newspaper and look at CMHC. It is not the fault of the people who work there, the permanent civil servants, Crown employees or whatever they are called. It is because of the Liberal government of this country that they have been brought to such a low estate.
Now, what makes me say that? I do not like to say that. I do not like to have to say this. What makes me say it is the fact that everywhere one looks in the country, these kinds of things are breaking out. From the Rudnicki affair-Rudnicki, the man treated shamefully by the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs-to urban transportation, to luxury hotels being financed by CMHC when there is no place for it. Anyone building a luxury hotel should be able to finance it himself through private means. There is York Place, Virginia Park in St. John's East. There is AHOP. AHOP is a living scandal, a running sore across the country. That is what AHOP is, with dingy contractors getting into CMHC and getting finances to build substandard hovels that are falling apart right across this country. They are subsidized by the Liberal government.
Name one.
I am naming one now, Virginia Park, and I am going to name another one in a few minutes.
Name a hundred, John.

There is Quigley Road, the whole thing. Everywhere one looks, the RCMP is probing here and probing there. We will not have a report until after the election, I
Housing
suppose. That is what is going on with CMHC across this country. It has come to this. Even now when we come to ordinary administrative detail, CMHC has weakened. They are weakened by the interference that they have had from this government. Everyone in the government should get at least ten years as a CMHC interferer, despoilers and molesters of CMHC.
Let us look at the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, RRAP. It was introduced in 1973. This will illustrate the cynicism of this government, the crass cynicism. My God, I wish they would go to the people tomorrow so that we could get them before the public and get them out before their cynicism spoils us all.
Right on.

It was introduced in 1973 to provide federal loans and grants to assist in the improvement and repair of substandard dwellings. It was an excellent program. Loans, part of which could be forgiven, were available to home owners and landlords who owned land in a particular neighbourhood improvement area or a specially designated area of the country. It was excellent to rehabilitate present housing stock. That was in 1973. Then it is announced that there are going to be some changes. It is announced by the government because it knows there is a big demand across the country for this. The government wants to pretend it is now going to become available to everyone, no matter where they live. So, the minister made a dramatic announcement that from now on the program is going to be universal, and there are several other changes. Landlords get done in a bit. They are not going to get direct loans, and they are not going to get as much forgiveness as before. Otherwise the program is going to carry on, but it is going to be universal.
When some members of the public hear that, they naturally expect "universal" means that everyone is going to be entitled to get a RRAP home improvement loan of $10,000 with $3,750 forgiveness, no matter where he lives; that one no longer has to live in a NIP area. That is the impression given by the minister of state for urbane affairs or profane affairs.
Then our astute housing critic comes across a memorandum from R. V. Hession, who is in charge of CMHC, to the hon. minister, dated January 3. It gives the lie to what the minister has said and shows the utter depravity of this government. It is a depraved government. I hate to mention that to you, Mr. Speaker. I do not want to shock you, sir. You do not realize, sir, what you have been associating with.
Order, order!

What did Mr. Hession say to the minister? He said this:
The 1979 capital budget is $56 million. We will need $37 million to maintain activity in the existing designated areas where work has already begun. A further $3 million will be needed to deal with areas already designated but where work has not started.
That is $40 million. He continues:
This leaves $16 million of the 1979 budget for new initiatives.

March 6, 1979
Housing
How far will $16 million go across the great Dominion of Canada to bring the RRAP program to the rest of the housing areas of Canada? He goes on to say:
However, 68 areas have submitted final applications for designation under the 1978 rules. After the new law comes into effect, they will not need order in council designation, but they will warrant some priority attention. These 68 areas will require at least $7 million. Thus only $9 million for some 2,250 units remains for work under the terms of the new program-
So, this is not a universal program. There is enough money in 1979 for 2,250 units, outside those already committed. It is a fairly modest amount, which Mr. Hession says it is. He points out that neither the industry nor the municipal delivery system can deal with a universal program, and that in a specific sense, anyone any day of the week cannot walk into a municipal office and be served.
When the minister got this memorandum on January 3, did he come out with a release the next day to tell Canadian people this truth? He did not. He continued his deception. He continued his false impressions. He continued his falsehoods until this was brought out by our housing critic, the lady who is going to be the minister of housing in our new great administration and bring into the House the mortgage interest deductibility. Herself and our finance minister will be fighting to the death to see who introduces it first. Maybe they will do it both together.
The letter goes on and talks about the number of units we need. Over two million housing units are in need of modernization. Over a ten-year period there are 200,000 to 400,000 which need serious upgrading, units occupied by lower income people. The letter goes on to say that we can do about 20,000 units a year. So, that is ten years just for just 200,000, not to talk about the two million, the two million homes where the minister has tried to give the impression that they are going to be eligible immediately for RRAP assistance: $10,000 to repair the home and $3,750 forgiveness. That is the kind of sleevenery with which this government hopes to stay in power. Well, it is not going to work. Mr. Hession goes on in his letter to talk about recent CMHC staff cuts which would make the servicing in municipalities very, very difficult. Therefore, 1979 will need to be devoted carefully to making inroads in existing designated areas, not new areas.
This is the most astounding document ever produced to refute and show how a minister attempted to deceive parliament and the Canadian people, and the man is still in the cabinet. That gentleman is still in the Government of Canada, in the cabinet. That shows the standards the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has. When one of his ministers is revealed to be deceiving the Canadian public and parliament, he allows him to stay in his cabinet, and then has attached a ten-year plan to modernize and rehabilitate Canada's housing stock.
Mr. Hession further goes into the details. One can see here a public servant who is trying to do his job, surrounded by depravity and deception and deceit. He is trying to do his job. He sets out the problem. At page 2 of his letter he said the following:

Accordingly, the policy of universal eligibility in urban areas has been adopted by the federal government. This will come into effect after Parliament has passed the bill-
He goes on to say:
It should be stressed that universal eligibility does not mean that anyone in Canada who feels they are in need of aid will automatically be served. At the moment, some 20,000 units are being rehabilitated annually. Rehabilitation is a complex process in which inspection, cost management, and consumer protection must all be undertaken with great care.
He goes on to point out how there is no possible way that there could be a universal program, and that they must assign priority and deal with those with the greatest needs first. He sets out three factors. 1 have not got the time to go into all of this. He sets out a ten-year plan to rehabilitate and modernize Canada's housing stock, following consultation with the provinces and so on.
The president of CMHC is an honest man trying to do his job. He is treading through the mire. He is treading through the muck, the worst kind of political chicanery that a government of Canada ever went through or ever put public servants through. He ends up with "this all sounds technical". It is not technical. It all sounds truthful. So, that is what we are dealing with in RRAP.
I tell the people of Newfoundland now, "You are not eligible for RRAP. They haven't got the money to give you the RRAP. It is only you people who are already in designated areas that have any chance of getting it this year. So, forget the lies that you have been told. There is no such program available to you."
Just before passing on to some incidents in my own district, I want to read this concoction from the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). It was delivered on February 19, 1979 at the annual meeting of HUDAC. HUDAC? HUDAC was the minister. He was speaking of HUDAC. This is what he said at page 21. He was trying to argue that the mortgage interest deductibility policy of the Progressive Conservative party, the new policy of the new government of Canada, should not be carried into effect. He is green with envy, so he trots out a tax credit scheme. I did not see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) dancing around the country shouting, "Billions for the tax credit scheme. This is going to be $5 billion or $6 billion." No, he certainly kept his mouth shut about that one.
After talking about this great tax credit scheme, which will not make any distinction between owners and tenants because none of them are going to get it, there never will be a scheme, he said this:
To introduce any general program, however, that seeks to redistribute income for shelter purposes, requires a very substantial commitment of government funds.
This is the first peak of truthfulness we see in this speech.
As a minister of the government in power, I do not have the advantage of being able to advocate prodigality on the one hand and retrenchment and restraint on the other.
Why not? Every other minister in the government is doing it. Is this the only minister forbidden to make these little
March 6, 1979

distinctions, to advocate prodigality on one hand and retrenchment on the other? But he says:
I do believe that in the near future, as soon as our economy permits-
That is a way out, Mr. Speaker, because if this crew were kept in power the economy would never permit this to be done. He went on to say:
-we should adopt a shelter allowance system that will provide assistance to home owner and tenant alike, through payment of a tax credit for shelter expenditures exceeding a certain percentage of income.
He is a wizard of weaseling, a weasel hoarding wizard of the cabinet when he can try to pretend to be introducing a great tax credit program and then say we will adopt it in the near future, as soon as our economy permits. We should adopt it so that when they are re-elected, if they are re-elected, they can say they never promised it in the first place because everybody knew the economy would never improve with them in power. That is as despicable as what that minister and his predecessors have done to what was once an excellent housing corporation. The Minister of Defence (Mr. Danson) was once the minister of state for urban affairs. The rot set in when he was there, and it has become far worse. I must say it has become even worse after the minister left. He is now Minister of National Defence, and the rot has set in there.
Now I want to come to AHOP. My friend, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), has put before the House what happened in Virginia Park and the AHOP program. He spoke about the fantastic conditions, the brick deterioration, the absolute lack of any standards of upkeep, of maintenance, of the housing that was put up in this area under AHOP by CMHC. When their inspectors had passed these inferior materials and standards, it was an insult to offer the people in Virginia Park, the low income residents there, additional loans to have their houses repaired so they would be in the state in which they should have been in the first place when the contractor sold them their homes financed by CMHC. They were going to charge them an interest rate on the loans. Well, that will not happen. They will get a far better offer than CMHC is making them before this is all over. These people have been put upon by the national housing agency which should never have permitted those units to be sold unless they were in proper condition to be sold.
It may be that private entrepreneurs can get away with it by saying, "Let the buyer beware." The private seller might be able to get away by using that old slogan, but the government cannot say "let the buyer beware" when the government is involved, and when the government has inspectors. The people of this country think that a CMHC inspector inspects and that what has been inspected is fit and proper when they buy it and assume a CMHC mortgage.
So I support my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East, and I support the Virginia Park Home Owners Association when they say that CMHC should put these dwellings into proper condition no matter what it costs them, without them lending any money to these people, with no increase in their mortgages or their responsibilities. There are serious allegations that the contractor, Brenjay Construction, bribed
Housing
CMHC inspectors. That is even a greater reason for this to be the case. When a contractor uses a corporation to do one job and a second corporation to do another job, and third corporation to do still another job, it is no good CMHC saying they can do nothing about it. These people now can only sue the corporation which built those homes, without the assets, and nothing left in it.
CMHC can police that, because they can say to the contractor, "You did a shobby job. You have incorporated another company, but never come to us for a mortgage loan again or mortgage financing until you have fixed up the first project." That is all they have to do. They should tell them, "Never again will you get CMHC financing until you have fixed up the situation which you have created in Virginia Park." That is all they need to do. Never mind the legalities, the legal struggle. CMHC is responsible, CMHC has to fix up the Virginia Park situation of the home owners who have been taken to the cleaners in purchasing these dwellings and assuming mortgages from CMHC, believing that CMHC had done a proper job.
It is not the old CMHC, Mr. Speaker, now that its morale is gone, with the hot-shot builders looking around their shoulders for hot-shot ideas from their political bosses. They have been ruined in every political sense of the word, and changed from a star agency to one for which we now feel sorry. They no longer seem able to administer properly even the humdrum task they have in my own district of St. John's West, in Kilbride in the Gould's. There is an instance here when in January some 150 to 250 home owners who bought AHOP homes in Kilbride suddenly got a notice from CMHC telling them that their monthly mortgage payments were increasing up to $80 a month because the municipal taxes had increased. When this was looked into, it was found that the municipal taxes had not increased at all, there had been no increase in either municipal assessment or taxes over the last three years in the St. John's metropolitan board area under which Kilbride comes.
What had happened was that originally someone got the wrong information that taxes were going to be $96 to $126 a year on these homes. When the tax bills were sent a year later for the true amount of the tax, in some cases it was $254 a year, CMHC paid the taxes to the St. John's metropolitan area board but did not pass this on to the mortgagors and did not let them know. They let it go for three years. Then, in January of 1979, they gave these home owners notice that starting April 1 they had to pay vastly increased monthly amounts on their mortgage until all the arrears in their municipal taxes, of which they knew nothing, were repaid. They told them they had to repay all the arrears this year, in 1979.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these are people in straitened economic circumstances who took over these homes because of the Assisted Home Ownership Program. These are low income and lower middle income people. In some cases when the true municipal taxes are added to what they have to pay, they are no longer even eligible for the AHOP assistance because they do not have sufficient income for that. But along comes

March 6, 1979
Housing
CMEIC, having made this mistake-it is a mistake of the computers or a mistake in the office, but it is their mistake- and they say, "We want you to start paying on April 1 vastly increased monthly payments. We want you to pay interest on the arrears in municipal taxes that you have not known about for three years."
Think of the audacity of that, Mr. Speaker. They are telling these people, "We did not tell you about these municipal taxes, we gave you the wrong figures, we did not collect them from you, we paid them. Now we are going to charge you interest on those arrears that you owe us." These people did not know there were arrears. These are innocent mortgagors, and they want them to pay the arrears back in 12 months.
I have written to the minister today and, if he has any sense, he can give me an affirmative answer to my letter or this bill will not be going through for months yet. Never mind a week or two weeks, a month, six months. If I could save some innocent 150 home owners in Newfoundland $1 a month, I would keep this bill going for six months, and no amount of squealing by the hon. gentlemen opposite would change my course. I would filibuster within the rules of the Elouse and I would have the House leader of the NDP advise me on the rules. I would be the first speaker to answer the government on third reading and 1 would go on for ten weeks, easily. I can tell you that, Mr. Speaker. I would check every house from here to Vancouver.
Another Rodriguez.

I have asked the minister to put off the date of April 1 because it is too soon. Every one of these people has to meet with CMHC officials and go over their accounts, have them verify them and check them with the municipal authorities, so they cannot start paying for the increase on April 1. They should forget their arrears and interest on taxes which they never knew they owed. The arrears and the interest should be forgotten about. In some cases these people should be given two years, and in other cases five years, in which to pay their arrears on taxes, depending on their income, if in fact they should pay any arrears on taxes. They are certainly going to be arguing that they should not be paying any of these arrears because they are the fault of CMHC and its administrative practices.
What has CMHC come to? It has been so overburdened by government changes of policy, by the introduction and cancellation of haphazard programs that the administrative processes of the organization, an admirable organization at one time and still capable of being so, are breaking down. Everywhere you look across the country there is a breakdown in the simple administrative processes of this important government agency, and it is hon. members opposite who have allowed and caused this to happen.
In the particular case I am talking about now there was another amusing incident, I suppose you could call it: CMHC did not pay municipal taxes on time and was assessed interest

by the municipality. Then CMHC sent the bill to the people down there who I shall be asking to vote for me in a few days or a few weeks or a few months, if this government ever gets up enough guts to go to the Governor General and get a dissolution so that we can put an end to their miserable tenure. They sent bills to the tenants asking them to pay the interest the corporation had to pay to the municipality because it was late in paying its taxes. Mr. Speaker, they can forget it. They are not going to get these interest payments because CMHC did not pay the municipality on time.
There is another problem I have discovered; it is similar to that of the Virginia Park Home Owners Association. I am told now that the quality of the workmanship in these homes is atrocious. The roofs leak, there is condensation inside and outside the walls, there is water everywhere, the windows don't fit, the doors won't close, and CMHC inspectors do not want to have anything to do with it. So there is another group of AHOP homes where the people who bought them are extremely dissatisfied. In some cases the contractor took the telephones and installed them against a beaverboard wall with nothing behind it. When you dialed a few numbers on your first day in the house the telephone fell off the wall. I suppose 1 cannot hold the minister responsible for that although I would like to. Was he down there at the time, I wonder? This is the kind of thing that is happening.
Why should lower income people who are being assisted to own their own homes have all this happen to them? It happened to them because there was not sufficient inspection by CMHC, because they moved into the program too quickly, because they did not take enough care, because the whole administrative structure of CMHC appears to be floundering.
I have written to the minister. He will get this letter tomorrow. I am hoping his parliamentary secretary is making notes and will see that this matter is looked into. When we get into committee, when I get back here on Thursday, I hope I shall receive some kind of "billet doux" so that I can tell these people who are going to see officials of CMHC on March 19, 20 and 24 just what attitude the minister is taking. CMHC has said they cannot do these things unless directed by the government.
NIP is a program which was very much used in St. John's, Newfoundland. They took good advantage of it, and in my own district of St. John's West several NIP programs have turned out very well. There have been others in mid-town St. John's and in St. John's East. Now NIP has gone and we are to have something called Community Services. But this will come in very slowly and there is a lot of discontent across the country at the way in which the government tried to fool the governments and the municipalities with regard to the new Community Services program. They tried to pretend it would be a vast expansion of the NIP program, but it was not. They nipped the NIP program; there is not going to be as much in the Community Services program as there was in the NIP program, though there will be more in future years when this government will not be here to be accountable for its promises-or there is going to be more if we can find any money
March 6, 1979

in the treasury to make sure that these promises are kept. One thing is for sure: the Liberal government will not be keeping them.
When I was getting ready for this debate I wanted to look up a quotation on housing from some kind of eminent gentleman. As hon. members know, 1 speak Chinese fluently. So, looking through my volumes of Chinese literature I came across this saying of Confucius-it seems to me I heard something from a confused lady on the other side of the House. I said "Confucius", not "confused".
Oh, oh!
We are going to miss the hon. lady in the next parliament. She is not going to be here.
You will miss me because you won't be here.
Oh, oh!

Is that a threat? Anyway, the quotation reads, "The strength of a nation is derived from the integrity of its homes." Well, Mr. Speaker, if that is correct, our nation has become pretty darned weak because our homes do not have too much integrity unless we have built them ourselves and got our own money for doing it. But if we are members of the struggling working class or the lower middle class and we had to go to an AHOP housing program to get a roof over our heads, to move out of an apartment, then the integrity of our homes is very much in question. I have heard members from right across this nation, from British Columbia to Manitoba to Newfoundland, describe what is happening to their electorate under the AHOP program. No wonder there is a high rate of foreclosures in connection with that program. I am hoping I have enough time to allow me to continue.
Go on!

The RRAP program I was discussing earlier sets a maximum of $10,000-that is all you are allowed to spend on any one home. Some months ago I suggested to the minister that $10,000 was not enough, especially in the case of an older home which needed to be renovated and repaired, and that the ceiling should be raised to $15,000. This has been the experience in St. John's.
I also drew attention to some crazy CMHC regulations having to do with certain building materials. Those regulations should be changed. I do not have the name immediately available to me but there is a building material, some kind of plaster you have to mix with water, and there is a factory here in Ottawa which manufactures it. CMHC stipulates you have to bring it to Newfoundland mixed with Ontario water; we are not allowed to mix it with Newfoundland water. So we have to pay a couple of hundred dollars in freight charges to ship this material, instead of paying $20. In other words, freight rates are about ten times as much as they should be because we have to pay to bring in a lot of Ontario water. I pointed out to the minister that there is one commodity we have a plentiful supply of in Newfoundland, and that is water. We do not need
Housing
to pay freight charges on Ontario water. We get watered on enough by Ontario. I have not had an answer saying whether the regulations will be changed or not. As I say, Mr. Speaker, the maximum amount available under the program should be raised if the scheme is to be effective.
There is another program I want to talk about-the CHIP program, the "Canadians hosed by parliament" program as I call it. This is one of the home insulation programs. That is the program one of the hon. members opposite was talking about. He tried to make out that mortgage interest deductibility was somehow anti-French-Canadian. It is a funny thing, everything we do on this side is supposed to be anti-the-French-fact or anti-French-Canadian or anti-Quebec. These gentlemen who are so much in favour of national unity never stop trying to spread their poison, whether in this chamber or outside. When it came to this CHIP program, what did they do? They arranged it so that the program in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island was different from that applicable to the rest of Canada.
Did we get up and say it was an anti-French-fact program, an anti-Quebecois program, an anti-bilingual program because Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia were being treated differently? We did not. We do not want to slither our way into power by playing that game. They introduced a program which discriminates against eight provinces in favour of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. If you live in Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island you can get a grant to help you instal insulation in your home, but if you live in the other provinces you get a loan which you have to pay back. I do not have time to discuss all these programs.
That is what I call a discriminatory program, not a mortgage interest deductibility program that is going to apply to every householder in Canada no matter where he lives. How can that be said to be discriminatory? A program is discriminatory that lays down one set of rules for one province and a different set for the other. That is the 1977 program which has been an immeasurable failure, Mr. Speaker. You get a taxable grant of up to $350 to insulate your home, that is in eight provinces, but down in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island you get a $500 grant, non-taxable. That is discrimination. If you want to talk about whether the Quebe-cois home owner is being discriminated against, yes, he is. This government discriminated against him because this government said, "If you want to insulate your home and you live in Quebec you are going to get $350 in a grant to help you, taxable; you have to add it to your taxable income. But, if you live in Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island you are going to get a $500 grant non-taxable, not added to your taxable income, and you do not have to pay tax on it." The result of this program was that the demand was far short of expectations.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Gillespie) says he has got an energy program. This is supposed to be part of it,

Housing
the conservation program, this disgrace, this CEIIP program. I suppose it was a chip program, Mr. Speaker. It was a gyp program, it was a gyp against the eight other provinces. We hear that the hon. gentleman wants to make energy an issue. The government wants to make energy an issue. I hope they do make energy an issue, Mr. Speaker. They will wish that they had not. I hope they make housing an issue.
So this is the sorry story that we have to speak about here tonight, Mr. Speaker, with failure after failure by this government, caused by political interference of every sort and description. We have the York Place affair in Hamilton with bribery, political intervention, cover-up, questionable lending practices, and we have not heard the last of that yet. That is in the courts and being investigated. It always takes years to investigate these. We have the hotel stories where people's money went. Imagine a government housing agency lending money to a luxury hotel, the Quai d'Orsay here in Ottawa, and on and on it goes. All the hotels we were promised were in good financial shape and they have gone bankrupt one after the other. The new Howard Johnson Hotel in Montreal, insured by CMHC, went into bankruptcy. On and on it goes, and whenever you ask the minister a question all he does is double talk.
The minister has got the most twisted mind I have ever come across, if it could be called a mind. Whatever it is, it is twisted, badly injured; it is damaged, it is a mind that has been used to molest CMHC.
There is the Cloverdale Park housing complex in Montreal where again there are a lot of low income earners, and again a lot of difficulty. CMHC is selling the complex to the private sector, and nobody knows about that until they see it in the newspaper. I have mentioned Virginia Park. I mentioned Kilbride and what happened there to 150 home owners, and the CHIP program, a disaster. Then we have the denial of civil rights to Walter Rudnicki, who was fired in 1973, a complete and utter denial of civil rights for he was successful in a lawsuit, was to be reinstated and found to be wrongfully dismissed. This government does not care about somebody being wrongfully dismissed. This government does not care about anybody's civil rights being trod on. It does not care at all.
Urban transportation-we won't even mention that because that is again political cynicism at its greatest. We have the minister letting Liberal MPs and politicians announce when loans are going to be made, or funds are going to be given to a riding, or grants under the municipal incentives grants program. No wonder-
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may continue with unanimous consent. Does the hon. member have unanimous consent?
Agreed.
No.

Mr. Speaker, any housing policies should have begun, instead of after the fact legislation such as this, with objectives and premises whose projections into the future were based on a clear assessment of the present situation in which we now find ourselves. Too often I have heard objectives stated in the negative, determined from limitations and reduced expectations, in the hope that Canadians will happily settle for, not necessarily the form of shelter that they desire, but rather some limited grey matchbox shelter which this government says they should want to live in. Too often I hear politicians and bureaucrats say that the cost of land, labour, capital, and taxes makes it unrealistic to expect that most young Canadians will ever have an opportunity to own their own homes. Governments then, given this premise, began to mass produce multiple matchboxes in order to meet dwelling number targets. This process needs to be reversed.
I say to young people, "Yes, within the productive span of your life, if home ownership is your goal, and I hope that it is the goal of every young Canadian, then the opportunity for you to reach that goal will be made available to you." We are a nation of vast opportunities and a nation with all the raw materials required for the building of housing to meet this objective of young people. We have much lumber for our houses, in fact so much that we export most of it. We have iron for nails, and sand for glass and insulation, and we have skilled labour, much of which sits idly unemployed. We have all these things in a country with one of the highest per capita incomes in the world. Of course we say, "Young man, go out and build your house; build a home in which you can raise a family and help to build this country. You can do it," we say to our young people, "that is provided, of course, provincial, municipal and federal governments and bureaucracies can be cleared out of your way."
My father built his first house out of prairie sod. My grandfather built his first house out of the rocks he picked off the land before he began to cultivate it. Believe it or not, somehow my father and my grandfather managed without the help of a zoning by-law, a land-use contract, a design panel, a building permit, a certified architect, an engineer, an electrical inspector, a plumbing inspector, and a framing inspector. Somehow they even managed without underground wiring, ornamental street lighting, 66-foot paved roads and five-foot concrete sidewalks. In fact, believe it or not, they even managed to move into their homes without first obtaining an occupancy permit from the local government.
Naturally they had other hardships. As well as governments and bureaucracies to do without, they also managed to do without paying 45 per cent of their disposable income to the government in taxes. Although it has, of course, had a few wires and central heating added, my grandfather's house still stands today, a symbol of individual initiative and integrity of both those who dreamed it and those who built it, and I can assure this House that my grandfather's house will be standing long after these AHOP disasters have crumbled into dust.
March 6, 1979

I am not suggesting that we go back to those days as such, obviously not. What I am saying is that government bureaucracy and over-regulation have destroyed individual initiative, incentive, and inhibited the individual's capacity to build. Integrity and quality craftsmanship, so lacking in today's AHOP home, are not values that are necessarily dead. They are in fact taught and learned values that can be rekindled. In our time integrity and quality craftsmanship can best be ensured through the principle of builders' long-term guarantees or warranties, as opposed to expensive, sand in the gears government inspection and regulatory bureaucracies.
My colleague just spoke and said a lot of faults in AHOP housing units relate to the fact that inspection was inadequate. We would not have required that inspection if, in fact, those houses had warranties with them, and had builders who were willing to stand behind their products. That is the kind of thing we need, not more and more sand in the gears bureaucracy which requires inspection after inspection after inspection. We require builders with integrity who will provide guarantees and stand behind the houses they are building.
The expression buyer beware can be made more meaningful through consumer education in the longer term, and in the shorter term moral suasion could be used, in other words the withdrawal of funding from offenders. We have heard tales here tonight from Newfoundland and I will be telling of people in British Columbia who have built their homes, and have tried to call the builder only to find out that the builder has moved on. We need a new bankruptcy act to prevent that old shell game.
We also need measures that will strengthen buyer protection. Mortgage money could be facilitated through a mortgage exchange corporation and by allowing and encouraging insurance, trust and pension funds to expand their investment portfolios into mortgages. More disposable income could be put into the hands of buyers through mortgage deductibility. Bureaucracy could be dismantled and deregulated, and duplication of effort between governments could be negotiated out of existence. I say, "could be". Apprenticeship programs and school curriculums could be revamped to create more competent and knowledgeable craftsmen. Municipalities could be assisted in land assembly, in the financing of trunk sewer and water lines. And the list of what could be done goes on and on.
Instead of the government trying to create an environment wherein the individual is competent to buy or build his own home, an environment where individual enterprise finds incentive through removal of government barricades and the availability of capital, particularly capital from the private sector, the government continues to interfere in the market place with consistent bungling and blundering. The AHOP program has to be the most classic example.
I would like to tell hon. members of a couple of such examples which exist in my own community. I met John Godmaire of Surrey the other night just as he was preparing to
Housing
take his son out to the scout troop which he leads. John took me through his house and showed me the wall between the kitchen and the living room and how that wall had pulled away from the ceiling and dropped. I have seen normal settlement to the extent of a hairline crack along the top of the plaster or which necessitated some minor adjustment to the wall, but what I saw in John's house was that the wall between the kitchen and the living room had dropped more than one inch. This house is an AHOP house, and this was only one of the problems.
In addition to the wall falling, the conduit wire leading from the electrical heating unit was drooped over the copper water pipes. This wire came down from a register through the floor and was wrapped completely around the copper water pipe tubing. The copper water pipe tubing, by the way, was wet with condensation. One does not have to be an engineer to know the danger which is inherent in that type of construction.
I cannot understand how it could have happened. I cannot understand how a builder could have been so negligent, let alone it being inspected. No one could have inspected this house, because it just is not possible. The next door neighbour could not have inspected it.
The dog did not inspect it.

No, the dog did not inspect it, because even a dog would have known better. The wiring which should have run through the plates and through the studs, instead was jammed in right behind the plaster board, and the plaster board was bulging out. Not only was the plaster board bulging, but it was absolutely wet from condensation. The windows were frosted over. I once lived in an older home on the prairies and I can remember waking up in the morning to find frost a half inch thick on windows, and I took it for granted that houses were built that way. But a modern house built today should not have an inch of frost on the windows, especially if it is a house located in British Columbia where the climate is not very cold and where there is very little frost.
I have documented this case and I have slides to illustrate this disaster. There was inadequate ventilation. The previous speaker talked about the phone which pulled out of the wall. In this case there was a railing going down the stairs which was merely screwed into the plaster board. There were no studs behind the screws, and the first time someone walked down these stairs they put their hand on this rail and it fell off. They were lucky they were not injured. These are little things which a contractor with any skill at all would have seen and corrected.
All John wanted for his family, Mr. Speaker, was a decent, sound, but inexpensive home in which to raise his family, and built in such a way so that he could go out at night and get involved in the community and the organizations, to work in a very good way and be the good kind of citizen his parents taught him to be. All he received, however, was a compounding debt, a depreciating investment, and shoddy, cheap and inadequate workmanship.

Liberal workmanship.

March 6, 1979
Housing
Yes, Liberal workmanship, the responsibility of this government and of this minister opposite,
Is the government also to blame if a marriage breaks up?

I am glad that the hon. member for Vancouv-er-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) has put her remarks on record in my speech, because I am going to send them out to British Columbia and say, "That is the attitude this government has." That is why these houses are built in this manner, because of this kind of sarcastic, non-caring attitude. Is she intending to go out and fix this house? I invite you to come to Surrey with me and I will show you this disgrace because I would like to see what you would do about it. Will she stand up and speak-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I would invite the hon. member to address himself to the Chair.
Who built the house?

Listen to the sarcastic ministers over there and let Hansard record their response.
Sheridan Myers is a railway worker in his late thirties and father of three young children. Sheridan and his wife Betty, salt-of-the earth Canadians, assumed a $39,500 mortgage plus a CMHC loan of $5,900 to buy their AHOP home in Mission, B.C. They put in a great deal of gardening, and they really worked hard and cared for their house. If one walks into that yard, they will see the loving care which went into that garden and how they tried to make that house in such a way that they could be proud of it as most Canadians want to be proud of their house. After a great deal of hard gardening and $17,000 in monthly payments, Sheridan and Betty found that CMHC was selling houses which had defaulted under AHOP next door, the same house that they had paid $39,500 for was now going for $32,000. Next month Sheridan's monthly mortgage payments will go up to $408 and then up by another $120. Unfortunately he finds himself temporarily unemployed, like thousands of other Canadians. He had great hopes for his home; then he found that his payments would be going up and his disposable income going down.
The frustration of Sheridan is undoubtedly shared by many AHOP home owners whose incomes are not rising with inflation and whose equity is falling. Up until a few months ago the Vancouver CMHC office did not have a market analysis branch, so 15 per cent of the units built between 1973 and 1978 are unsold today.
Would you say that again?

It amounted to 15 per cent of the units built. It is not a one-year mistake, but they kept making it year after year and, as a result 15 per cent of the units built between 1973 and 1978 are sitting unsold.
Empty.

As a result of the overbuilding and the inflationary price rise in moderately priced housing due to

AHOP, people who bought an AHOP home have no equity at all despite having made payments of several thousands of dollars.
To add insult to injury, CMHC sold a house in Sheridan's development, the same type of house for which he paid $40,000, for $32,000. Two weeks later the speculator who bought the house for $32,000 sold it for $37,000. The government gave away $5,000. Fortunately, Sheridan was able to sell his house for $38,000 and get out with only a slight loss-a slight loss in dollar bills, but what kind of a loss in human and social circumstances? What kind of loss of hope for him? He took the responsible attitude. While so many others just walked out of their homes and left the government with the burden, he stayed and paid.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what is going to be done about this nightmare? The Sheridans and the Johns and thousands of others across the country are disappointed, frustrated, bitter. The builder does not seem to care. He has received his money and has probably started a new project under a new company name in order to escape the responsibility for poor workmanship. He says, "That company is now broke; we cannot guarantee your warranty or bring your house up even to the basic standards." After the fact, CMHC comes in and says there is nothing they can do because the builder is now bankrupt-or says he is. When they are told the builder is in business across the street they reply, "There is nothing we can do about that; that is a different company." The builder does not care. He is not going to do anything for them. He is not going to take that wire and unwrap it from that water pipe; he is not going to fix that rail on the wall.
What about the lender? surely the person who put up the money is concerned about the shoddy job? The lender pays little attention. He has not bothered about the risk because, if they walk out, what is the difference to him? Central Mortgage and Housing has guaranteed his risk. The person who loaned the original money does not care and is not going to put any more money in the house. When he gets his out, that is all he cares about.
Central Mortgage and Housing should care, but they cannot do anything about it. They do not really care because they can go on subsidizing with magnanimous indifference. They can subsidize again and again, pick up loss after loss, then walk out of it. What are we left with, Mr. Speaker? The person in the house has been done a serious wrong. He knows he has been wronged, and every Liberal on the other side of the House knows that the man I speak of has been wronged. Mr. Speaker, you know he has been wronged.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext: Do you?

You are darned right. Mr. Speaker has been paying attention and he knows. If the minister has not, he should. I hope he knows, because I would not want Mr. Speaker to get caught in one of these AHOP housing deals and
March 6, 1979

see it fall around him. Mr. Speaker, you had better listen. You had better pay attention.
We leave the poor Central Mortgage and Housing person-
And the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) laughs.
Of course the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) laughs. He sees no injustice in this.
He does not care.

He does not care. He lives in a big house. Why does he not listen to his constituents and hear some of these people cry? They do not have a bank to go to for credit. Their credit is being destroyed and they have to walk out of these houses. To appeal, they go to Central Mortgage and Housing where the poor civil servant is left holding the bag behind the desk. He hears their complaints and makes some suggestions, but the suggestions are no good because he cannot give them money or rebuild their house. He can do nothing for them. The government leaves the poor civil servant to take all the flack and all the agony of these people.
I hope that everyone sitting in an AHOP house tonight that is built in an inferior manner will hear me and go and see their member of parliament, or write to the minister or to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), inviting them to come and see their houses. I hope every one of them will do that. They should not call Central Mortgage and Housing but rather their member of parliament so that we can get some action on the floor of this House right now.
Call the Minister of Justice.
Call the Minister of Justice and say, "Where is this just society?" The only just opportunity is just an opportunity to make extra payment.
That is silly.
It wouldn't be so silly if it was you.
You are worse than he is.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the government and the future opposition thinks I am terrible. I am mad, Mr. Speaker. I am mad as can be that these poor, honest, upright Canadians are carrying the bag for this government once again. I can tell you it is so.
What nonsense.

If the government thinks it can sweep this problem under the carpet by simply terminating the program and omitting any corrective response in this legislation-if it thinks it can get away with that, it is mistaken. Some 130,000 homes were built under the AHOP program of which perhaps 53,000 are still empty, and more are becoming empty every day as people walk out of them.
Housing
Some Canadians are still satisfied because, fortunately, within that 130,000-and not because of the government- there were some responsible builders who wanted to make sure the quality of their houses was good. They built their houses strongly and well. If some houses can be built strongly and well for $47,000 in Vancouver, there is no reason why the house next door cannot be built to the same standard for the same price.
Many thousands of builders are unhappy, and many thousands of owners in AHOP houses tonight are unhappy. Many realtors are also unhappy. Their name has been sullied because of the houses and they are now taking the flack. They are just beginning to understand the problems. The walking out is just beginning. The problem will not go away, Mr. Speaker. Corrective measures will have to be taken by this government. Who will do the repairs or finance the corrections that are required to John's home and his neighbours' homes? Will these Canadians have to learn the hard way that their fate in the Liberal government was misplaced?
I should like to quote from an interview I had with Mr. Myers when I asked him:
Is this story that you're telling me your story only or typical of all the people in this subdivision who are having the same problem?
He replied:
That's right. If I walk away from here I'm just out and I have to rent for the rest of my life or until five or six years is up and they forget about my credit.
Well, there are a lot of people who have put a lot of work in a lot of houses. You look at some of them ... These are the people who are staying here and they are the people who are going to shoulder it and by rights we have just been taken to the cleaners.
I then asked him:
In other words, you are going to carry the mistake of the government. The government won't lose but you will.
He replied:
Yes, isn't that the way it always is?
Mr. Speaker, that is the way it always has been. That does not mean it is the way it is going to be or the way it has to be. If this government will not make the corrections in the next few days in this House, then they will have to be thrown out of office. Let this be one of the reasons that they are thrown out. Let the Johns and the Sheridans stand up and say they have had enough of this government.
We will make it right.
We will make it right. We will not leave the people to carry the burden of the government.
We care. They do not care.

The AHOP program was predicated on three factors, first, that inflation would assure that the value of a house would rise rapidly; second, that an individual's disposable income would increase, and third, that market demand would be such that an oversupply would not result and therefore devalue the price of AHOP homes. None of these factors turned out to be true. Inflation rose but house prices generally,

March 6, 1979
Housing
and specifically AHOP house prices, dropped. The individuals' income rose but so did his taxes. The hon. member who spoke ahead of me dealt with how taxes have risen. The taxes rose, the government failed to pay them, and now the owner is supposed to pay a penalty on top. His family expenses that were supposed to be in control relative to his disposable income have increased. In fact as his family grew it probably became more expensive to keep them month after month, not less expensive. His monthly house payments increased faster and faster as his disposable income failed to increase.
Market demand for all types of housing, particularly AHOP, softened, and because AHOP was the only game in town supply outstripped demand, lowering the value of AHOPs already purchased as well as over saturating the market with a product for which there was declining demand. The odds were stacked against the Sheridans and the Johns from the beginning because they had to bet on inflation. Their purchase was predicated on factors that might not necessarily occur and that in fact that did not occur.
The Fraser Institute of Vancouver did a critical study of AHOP houses. The results were very negative, Mr. Speaker. The major drawback to the program was the fact that in many instances interest indebtedness accumulated faster than principal payments. Because of this the borrower's underlying security might be marginally in excess of his total liability.
Let me give you a specific actuarial example. I have given you first of all the humanistic example of John and Sheridan. 1 have told you about their individual problems, and generally how they repeated them to me. But this is how accountants look at the matter. For example, take a housing unit costing $47,000 to purchase, with a $45,115 mortgage. The borrower, at the end of the first year, would have paid $5,210.76 in monthly mortgage payments. Of that amount $361.92 would be applied to the outstanding principal, leaving a balance of $44,753.08. This would be somewhat less than the original $45,000 the borrower paid. Meanwhile an interest reduction loan would have been secured during that same period. That is where the catch comes in. An interest reduction loan of $1,080 is secured bringing his total liability at the end of the first year to $45,833.
It is hard for the man in the street to realize that he can buy a house costing $45,115 at the beginning of the year and at the end of the year, after having paid $5,200 toward it, he suddenly finds he owes more than he paid at the beginning, which was $45,833. In the second year the outstanding mortgage balance would be $44,303 while his interest reduction loan would be increased to $1,944. This now brings the total indebtedness to $46,247. Bear in mind the original cost of the house was $45,115. By the end of the fifth year the mortgage outstanding would have decreased $42,769.23 while the home owner's total liability, which included the interest reduction loan of now $3,240, would be $46,009. After five years the owners' equity in the House would in fact be less. Fiver years later, after he has paid his payments faithfully month after

month, he now owes $46,009 on a house which he purchased originally for $45,115. He now wonders how that is possible.
Then comes the tragedy that this $45,000 debt has dropped in value to perhaps $32,000. If that is the case, as it was in the example I stated, the man has lost $16,000. He cannot reclaim it. He is stuck. He cannot move. All he can do is walk out, and leave the government holding the bag. At the same time he will be ruining his credit and losing hope of owning a home. We might say "Buyer Beware. He knew what he was getting into." But unfortunately Canadians do not understand the whys and wherefores of mortgages. What he got into was government deception. This situation occurs in all cases unless houses of this type appreciate in value.
This combination of rising total indebtedness with a minimum downpayment could place purchasers who are forced to sell in the untenable position of having insufficient equity to handle the transaction costs which include lawyers fees and agents costs. In other words, to get out of the situation, even if the individual walks out of the house, and tries to sell, he must still pay agents and lawyers fees over and beyond the debt he has accumulated on the housing unit.
A few years ago when housing prices were generally increasing, this was not a problem. If householders could not keep up the payments because of a change in economic circumstances, such as the loss of employment or perhaps lower than expected income increments, or perhaps they experienced a shift in social arrangements, for example, divorce or separation, these owners could just sell. But now with stable or depreciating house values in some markets, owners will have little in capital value on which to fall back.
As one builder who was delighted to sell his units by first renting them, said, "I know some of these families just have enough income to pay rent in much lower priced accommodation. There is no way they can handle the basic monthly mortgage requirement on a $47,000 home, much less all the other costs of home ownership, such as taxes, heat, water, and minimum maintenance, so I am happy to sell my units. But how the government can be a party to this is beyond me." How can the government allow someone to get so far over his head?
The combination of unsatisfactory improvements in equity and limited down payment-in Canada 86.4 per cent of AHOP purchasers secured ownership on the minimum downpayment of 5 per cent or less-left marginal purchasers with very little cushion and less opportunity for error. The hope, and for that matter their collateral, was the possibility that their homes would rise at a rate equal to or in excess of the rate by which assistance was withdrawn. Backing their trust in the future was an unwillingness to believe that anything could go wrong. People believed that somehow this government would give leadership. These people went along with the blind faith that nothing could go wrong. A program was set up on that basis. People surmised that property values would surely increase sufficiently to offset increased liabilities. One might have thought so, but practice has proven otherwise.
Again, to correct these weaknesses, the government revised the program. They have revised it so many times that not only
March 6, 1979

do the home owners not know that they are doing but neither does Central Mortgage and Housing, nor this parliament, nor the minister. No one knows what is going on. The person who knows is the individual who sees his house crumbling beneath him. He is the one who sees his debt increasing, his payments increasing, and the value of his house dropping. But they do not care.
The hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy) does not care.
Does the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy) care? I hope he cares but I hear him say that he does not care. Perhaps hon. members say people should look before buying.
He does care.
He does care.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege. I hope that the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott), who is the official critic for the opposition, could at least have the courtesy of not following members around as they speak just to get a few cheap political points on television.

Mr. Speaker, I am rather surprised the hon. member did not stand up to say that he, as a Liberal, cares about these people. But he stood up to care a little bit about politics. He has just made his maiden speech. I hope the hon. member and some of the other Liberals will care enough to stand up and speak out against the problems of AHOP housing. That is the kind of standing up that is demanded in this House. Stand up for these little Canadians and show them you care.
I could talk about the problems of AHOP 1978, but I see that I am running out of time.
Take all the time you want.
Oh, oh!

Listen to them over there. I say that 1 am running out of time, and they say good. I am pleased to hear hon. members say that, because they are worried. They know it hurts and they know I am right. They know there are thousands of people across Canada who are living in AHOP houses saying tonight, "Maybe we can get some help yet. Maybe there is some hope, and maybe things are not at a dead end." But hon. members over there do not care. The Liberals do not care.
It is evident that several families will be in a no-exit situation in these AHOP homes unless there occurs what a Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation official prescribes. This is the answer of the government. This is what Central Mortgage and Housing says, "Home owners, don't worry because there may be a sudden gust of inflation or a sharp reversal of present economic trends." I do not expect there will be a sharp gust of inflation. But the official was
Housing
right when he said there will be a sharp reversal of economic trends. That sharp reversal will come when the government on the other side is replaced.
For some home owners just walking away is cheaper than sticking around to try to pull out of the financial quagmire. The more vexing question is what will CMHC, as the carrier for insurance for nearly 100 per cent of these loans, do? The AHOP default rate is now running at 10 per cent and growing. What will they do with 15 per cent or 20 per cent? The minister hides the figures. I tried to get them for two years and could not. Either they did not know or they were hiding them.
If a 10 per cent default ratio is any indication of what can be expected under more severe economic conditions, CMHC will no doubt find itself with thousands of unwanted and unpaid for homes sitting on their doorstep. Since the only way to minimize this eventuality is to improve the marketability of AHOP units, they are trying to devise other items like graduated mortgage payment plans. That is just trying to buy time. It is trying to buy the people beyond an election, letting them think that they will somehow, through some magic formula, not have to pay the whole price of a house, that they can delay the payments forever, not recognizing that all it means is that their debt and interest are piling up greater and greater and they are getting further and further in. I can see the former minister smiling.
I am not smiling.

No, he is not smiling; he is crying. He should be crying because, unfortunately, he devised the program. I hope he is crying as he is listening to this speech. If he is crying, it may be that he cares a little bit, and that is what Canadians want to see from that side of the House, a little bit of caring, a little bit of correction.
What are they going to recommend now? Who is going to rebuild these houses. Who will finance them? Will they do something constructive like set up a bit of a fund and allow the people to repair their own homes to bring them up to a minimum, not maximum, CMHC standard? Will you give John Godmaire enough just to correct the mistakes the CMHC inspector did not see? Will you let him pay an electrician to come in and take the electric wire that is wrapped around the copper pipe with the water dripping from it, and change it so that his family can be safe and the house will not burn to the ground with the family in it? Will you do that little bit?
Don't just sit there shouting at me to tell you what to do. I am giving you some ideas. Where are your ideas? What are you going to do? You created all of these AHOP problems; how are you going to get us out of them? Don't delay the graduated mortgage program. Don't wait for a gust of inflation. Let's not keep hoping on the false premise that destroyed the program. It has not worked. Do not keep hoping that some day there will be a reversal and one day they will come through.

March 6, 1979
Housing
Don't just shove this program under the carpet. Don't just tell the people not to worry because we do not have AHOP any more and, therefore, there will be no more AHOP mistakes. That is what we keep assuring the people. What about the 130,000 homes already built? What about the 53,000 unoccupied? What are you going to do with them? What are you going to do for these people?
I agree with the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) that this bill should not go through this House until the government has come up with a method to help these people who have been cheated and deceived by this government, and who are receiving inferior workmanship and craftsmanship. I do not ask you to rebuild the houses. Just work a little bit on the ventilation and the heating.
Just give these people a little assistance and they will stay in their homes. In spite of the mistakes that have been made by the government, they will stay in them. They will care. Stop the roof from leaking and they will stay in the home. They would make the repairs, but they do not have the money to do it. The reason is that their monthly payment is going up this month to a rate they cannot afford because their disposable income did not reach that much this month.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-REASON DETAILED INCOME TAX RETURNS PLACED IN CUSTODY OF STATISTICS CANADA
NATIONAL REVENUE-REASON DETAILED INCOME TAX RETURNS PLACED IN CUSTODY OF STATISTICS CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as the response to my question regarding the Statistics Canada matter on February 23 was concerned, the minister stated at that time "our files are kept in strictest confidence". That may be true if you conveniently forget the fact that there is an ongoing responsibility for the files and the data under Section 23 of the Statistics Act, and while the minister in charge of Statistics Canada has acknowledged this from the beginning, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) seems more concerned with trying to evade his responsibility which is clearly set out in Section 23 of the Statistics Act.
The Minister of National Revenue should keep in mind that it is not that long ago that radio personalities were able to extract taxpayers' information from computers under the control of his department. Others share my misgivings, including the prestigious and respected Edmonton Journal which, in an editorial only a few days ago, made the following comment:
The prospect of Tory MP Elmer MacKay rooting through confidential government documents probably gives the Trudeau government nightmares.
What he found last week in the basement of a Statistics Canada office building ought to give us all a nightmare: 60 cardboard boxes full of tax returns and other documents, all marked "Confidential-to be destroyed."-
Industry Minister Jack Horner's observation in the House of Commons that "(Statistics) are taken and collected under the strictest and most confidential methods possible" may be quite correct. It's what happens later that has us worried.
Deputy Prime Minister Allan MacEachen's promise to investigate the incident was vital, as will be the government's assurances that Mr. MacKay's discovery revealed an isolated lapse of security that will not be repeated.
Canadians are concerned about Statistics Canada's incessant demands for information, its legal right to compel responses and the expanding use of social insurance numbers for identification. Proper guarantees of confidentiality are
March 6, 1979

timely and a prerequisite if this information-gathering system is to continue to function.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) has another responsibility. I am quoting from the Statistics Act, Section 23:
For the purposes of this act... the Minister of National Revenue shall cause to be sent to the Chief Statistician returns of imports and exports into and from Canada and details of the means of transportation used therefor, in such manner and at such times as the governor in council may prescribe upon the recommendation of the minister and the Minister of National Revenue.
I think it is important that the Minister of National Revenue, who is obviously making attempts to establish himself as a cutting and controversial figure, as evidenced by the memos he writes to himself, is spending more time trying to play Tiny Tim to his seatmate Burt Reynolds that in trying to get to the bottom of some of these difficulties mentioned in the Edmonton Journal. It is obvious, when you look at the data which has been supplied to the then minister over the years, that there has been an ongoing lapse of responsibility not, I suggest, as it has turned out, by the incumbent as far as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) is concerned but basically by the personnel and indirectly by the minister responsible for Statistics Canada.
I have here a report sent to the then minister some years ago by a man who is still, I believe, in the employ of Statistics Canada. It is a very comprehensive report and it deals with the types of security procedure which have been found so wanting recently. It talks about the storage and security of mental health statistics documents, it deals with the question of whether security precautions are necessary, it covers several pages, and I intend to make it available to the minister so that he can endeavour to find out what happened to this document which was submitted on August 22, 1966, outlining the same conditions as are causing Canadians such concern today.
This situation did not arise yesterday. Mental health records which are demanded by Statistics Canada are another matter of great concern, probably of even greater concern, on balance, than income tax information. I want to talk about the situation in which a letter was sent to a former minister, Jean-Luc Pepin. It stated that cards dating back to at least 1931 had been kept in an unlocked, unguarded room. This is in the same building as the forms I came across were in. They were piled helter skelter, freely available for inspection by any citizen. More recent cards have been stored in unlocked filing cabinets.
In 1968 the health and welfare division of DBS moved to No. 5 temporary building, the letter goes on to say. Some mental morbidity cards were stored in a room even though a vault was available a few feet away. More current cards were kept, as before, in unlocked filing cabinets. The door to room 2141 was kept open. A few flimsy cardboard boxes, lids open and containing notifiable cards, were also kept in this room. The question is, what has been done and what is the Minister of National Revenue going to do to exercise his responsibilities under the act. I see you are about to rise, Mr. Speaker. Has my time expired?
