speakeroldname: Mr. Yves Demers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue and Minister of State (Small Business)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-REASON DETAILED INCOME TAX RETURNS PLACED IN CUSTODY OF STATISTICS CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister reminded hon. members this afternoon, under the law Statistics Canada must have access to tax returns and the underlying principle of that requirement should be easily understandable.
In our system of government, Statistics Canada is the agency responsible for gathering and publishing statistical information on all aspects of Canadian society. The federal government, provincial governments and the private sector need reliable information on hundreds of aspects of our society.
The most important measure for a society is no doubt its income and the distribution of that income. Personal and corporate income tax forms sent to National Revenue for tax purposes are the best and most reliable source of information on incomes. If Statistics Canada were forbidden access to those returns, that agency would have to make major and costly surveys to gather the same information once again.
The general principle of the Statistics Act and even of the Income Tax Act is that an individual's business is his own business. If an individual has to provide information for tax or statistical purposes, the government must make sure that information is not made public.
On the other hand, governments and other organizations need over-all revenue information developed by the statistics system from income tax returns.
Therefore, parliament in its wisdom specifically provided that:
The chief statistician or a person so authorized by him may examine all reports, certificates, statements, documents or other records obtained for the Minister of National Revenue for the purposes of the Income Tax Act.
But since parliament also had a concern for the confidentiality of information submitted to Statistics Canada, it provided further that such information, when communicated to Statistics Canada, are subject to the same security rules as applied when they are collected.
Clearly, Statistics Canada employees must comply with the drastic confidentiality rules set under the National Revenue Act, which sets up penalties for officials or authorized persons who knowingly communicate or allow to be communicated information obtained for the purposes of the National Revenue Act.
For this reason Statistics Canada only publishes information on group revenues, without disclosing individuals' fiscal information. Those are legal provisions set forth in the National Revenue Act and the Statistics Act.

subtopic: POST OFFICE-STEPS TO IMPROVE DOOR TO DOOR DELIVERY
POST OFFICE-STEPS TO IMPROVE DOOR TO DOOR DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I asked a question of the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamon-tagne) on door to door mail delivery, a problem which in the last two or three years has become a festering sore for myself and my constituents. I must say that the Postmaster General has been very understanding and very supportive on this point. I am glad to see in the House tonight my good friend and colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General (Mr. Collenette), to respond to my question.
Essentially the answer was that there is the problem of restraint in government spending, as we have been told before. We all appreciate this, and we all support the concept of government restraint. But in this case the problem is somewhat different from any other. It is the question of a basic service that is not being provided to some Canadians. Also, there is the question of reallocation within particular departments. In this case it is the Post Office budget. Perhaps these things are not easy, but they are not impossible.
This situation is a rather unfortunate one in a number of ways. The business of not providing door to door mail delivery to some people, when the majority in the same area or neighbourhood are receiving this service, must be called discriminatory. In fact these people are making contributions to society. They are paying their taxes through the same tax system, but they are not receiving the same services which their neighbours receive who, in many cases, are just across the road. This is unfortunate in a time when we are concerned about the high unemployment rate, and when there are many, many programs at great expense to create employment, sometimes with difficulty. This is a natural situation in which to help the employment situation with the hiring of more letter carriers. This type of work is considered regular in our society. It would not be a short-term artificial creation of jobs through job creation programs. Also, there is a general feeling about the postal service these days. Admittedly there have been many problems, but in the case of door to door delivery it is an area which can be remedied easily.
I am informed the total cost would be approximately $24 million to hire enough extra letter carriers across the country to provide service for everyone. That may seem like a lot of money in individual terms, but it is relatively modest and not a large sum in terms of total government spending which amounts at the federal level to somewhat over $50 billion. There are a number of areas of possible savings. Many job creation programs come under the Department of Employment and Immigration. Of course they could be rearranged to provide some or all of this money. Something unusual which happened recently in government programs-and coincidentally the amount of money would be the same-was the proposal to provide perhaps $18 million to $20 million for professional NHL hockey arenas. It seems that is not a matter of very high

priority, certainly not compared to providing regular mail service.
All these matters would apply especially to constituencies like Halton. It is a typical suburban riding with a great many new addresses, subdivisions, and people upset about not receiving door to door mail delivery. The people of Halton voluntarily and good naturedly gave up the government job creation program, Canada Works, with the idea that it was not needed there as much as in some other areas. Yet, door to door mail delivery is an area of particular need. Other members of parliament have expressed this concern and have suggested remedies.
I feel justified in speaking at this time during adjournment debate because I have spoken at all levels: in this House, at various caucuses, and so on. We are at the point where something must be done. At this time of year there are more complaints because of the weather, the breaking up of winter. This is particularly difficult for old people and young children. For example, today I received a complaint from a constituent who said, "If we cannot get this kind of help, at least let's make the most of the situation."
Could some level of government perhaps not provide platforms, catwalks, wastebaskets and this type of thing until we can hire more letter carriers? The Postmaster General in his answer to me said this was a matter of high priority for him, and it was simply a matter now of money. He said it was up to the Treasury Board and the cabinet, and people are becoming very impatient, with good reason, some having waited up to two years. Some MPs suggest even longer. I think now it is time to stop talking about it, and time to act. I hope the parliamentary secretary can help in this respect. I hope the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) takes particular note.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subtopic: POST OFFICE-STEPS TO IMPROVE DOOR TO DOOR DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) for his concern in respect of this particular matter. I am not sure my answer this evening will do anything to allay his fears. In a sense he answered the question in his own statement. I am not sure what encouraging words I can give.
It is well-known that suburban areas in this country have expanded rapidly in the last three or four years, and generally in these new developments there are alternative services to door to door delivery. These services take the form of group boxes or general delivery. Therefore, the people living in these area like Halton are not without mail service, they merely have a different form of the service. It is obviously not the best service that we could hope for, but certainly it is the best possible service the Post Office can provide at this point in time while the Post Office takes steps to make improvements which Canadians in the rest of the country desire.
Though it is not possible to make any definite announcements at this time, the Post Office is looking carefully at those
March 6, 1979

areas in Canada which are most affected by the restraint on door to door delivery with a view to providing whatever service we can, best suited to each community. The Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) is not insensitive to the hon. member's respresentations or those of his colleagues, the hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne), the Minister of National Revenue and Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott), the Minister of State (Multiculturalism) (Mr. Cafik), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson), the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell), and others from the metropolitan Toronto area. There are many in the suburban fringes of Toronto who are faced with the same problem as the hon. member for Halton. Perhaps it is most acute in Halton, but it is something about which the Postmaster General is most concerned.
The problem the hon. member raised is one which I know the minister is looking at most seriously. We are trying to juggle resources in order to come up with some effective compromises. There are Canadians right across the country, not just in the metropolitan Toronto area, who do not have door to door service. The minister has mentioned on several occasions that the policy is national in scope and affects the ridings of many hon. members. I am sure the hon. member for Halton appreciates, as do most Ontario members in this House, that individual regions cannot necessarily be treated individually. One must have a national policy and apply it right across the board. All members are familiar with the restraint program of the government which affects the expenditures of all departments. In the Post Office, unfortunately, it is most visible, because door to door delivery in areas which are beyond existing letter carrier routes are the services which are affected.
I would like to assure the hon. member that the government has been exploring ways and means by which to provide this very visible service, as it does affect every riding in the country. There are no funds available at this time, but the Postmaster General is taking the matter up with his colleagues, and hopefully something can be done to improve the situation in the very near future.

subtopic: POST OFFICE-EFFECT OF CUTBACKS ON MAIL DELIVERY
POST OFFICE-EFFECT OF CUTBACKS ON MAIL DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I asked on March 1 is very similar to the question asked by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook). I put it to the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) in the following terms:
In every city in Canada there are tens of thousands of people living in newly built areas in the suburbs who do not get door to door delivery. Some of them have been waiting for three or four years.
I urged the minister to use his influence to try to persuade the government to allow him to hire people to deliver on a door to door basis; perhaps the 1,850 employees by which he proposes to reduce the number of employees in the Post Office department in the coming year.
Adjournment Debate
The minister's answer to me was very much like the answer he has given other hon. members. He said as reported at page 3711 of Hansard:
-I am aware of the fact that many growing areas, especially suburban areas, are without door to door service. I am also aware that in Scarborough, Calgary and other areas there is restraint in door to door delivery. I can assure the hon. member, as I said before, that as soon as money is available it will be my top priority in these urban areas to give Canadians door to door delivery.
I am not satisfied with the answer which the minister gave to me or the answer which was given to the hon. member for Halton by the parliamentary secretary. The fact is that there are tens of thousands of homes across the country in suburban areas which are not getting door to door delivery. I have been told that in the city of Edmonton there are 35,000 homes which are not getting door to door delivery. In the city of Calgary there are apparently 18,000 homes which are not getting door to door delivery. In my city of Winnipeg there are between 7,000 homes and 8,000 homes which are not getting door to door mail delivery. I do not have the figures for other major cities such as Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal, Halifax or Dartmouth, but I am sure that we are talking of several hundreds of thousands of homes. The people who have purchased homes in the newer areas of cities, not just my city of Winnipeg, but in every city across Canada, pay substantial amounts of money for those homes. In the last few years these people have probably paid more money than people who purchased homes in the older parts of cities. I do not believe that the people living in the newer parts of the cities should be considered as second-class citizens, but that is how they are being treated as a result of this phony policy of restraint of this government.
The parliamentary secretary and the minister have said that these people have service because they have the boxes. I wish the parliamentary secretary would come to Winnipeg in November, December, January or February, because he would see the kinds of conditions which these people must put up with, the minus 30 degree temperatures, three feet of snow, and a 25 or 30 mile an hour wind. Going to the boxes for the mail is no easy chore.
There are also the cases where these people receive registered letters and, as a result, must trot down to some post office which often closes at 3.30 in the afternoon and, as it frequently happens, both the husband and the wife are working from eight in the morning to four in the afternoon. When there is a parcel these people with boxes often travel three, four or five miles in order to get it from some regional post office.
The parliamentary secretary in reply to the hon. member for Halton said that the people in Halton were not the only people adversely affected, and he is right. He said that this freeze was part of a national policy. I want to say to the parliamentary secretary that a national policy which provides for a freeze on the hiring of letter carriers after tens of thousands of people have moved into these newer areas is dead wrong. I do not accept, nor will I ever accept, that there are people in this

March 6, 1979
Adjournment Debate
country who must be treated as second-class and third-class citizens.
The hon. member for Halton said that it would cost $20 million to provide letter carrier service for all the urban areas in Canada. I do not know if that figure is correct, but I intend to pursue that matter in the committee which deals with the estimates of the Post Office. However, the parliamentary secretary knows, as do myself and the hon. member for Halton, that there are many ways in which the government can save money if it must, but one of the worst ways of saving money would be not to expand the letter carrier service. I think that the people in the suburban areas, some of whom have waited as long as four years for letter carrier service, have waited too long, and I call upon the government to rescind the freeze order on the provision of letter carrier service, and to provide the people of these new areas with the same service as other urban citizens are getting from one end of Canada to the other.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was quite prepared to answer the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) on an entirely different matter. subtopic: POST OFFICE-EFFECT OF CUTBACKS ON MAIL DELIVERY
speechtext: Which I made on March 1.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subtopic: POST OFFICE-EFFECT OF CUTBACKS ON MAIL DELIVERY
speechtext:
Looking through the record I see that on February 22, I answered a similar question in response to the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). It is quite apparent that there is a different approach to this from the three major parties in the House. My colleague from Halton was most reasonable in talking about the problem and understood the constraints upon the system. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) spoke on this a couple of weeks ago. The Conservative party talks restraint, but when it comes down to the crunch it starts talking about deficits and providing mail service, notwithstanding the restraint program of the government. This clearly shows where the real sentiments of the Conservative party lie.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we have the hon. member for Winnipeg North giving the NDP view. The NDP view is-it is the classic NDP approach-that because we have a restraint program and because we recognize that not all people are getting the same quality of service, some are automatically second class citizens. That is the way the NDP gets votes across this country-by creating class division. That is an approach that I completely reject, but it is typical of the New Democratic Party. They do not recognize that there is a certain limit to the financial resources of the country. During the minority government of 1972-1974, the NDP pushed the government into all kinds of costly programs from which we are now extricating ourselves.
I think the hon. member would do a much better service to the cause of providing adequate mail service and letter carrier service across the country if he would adopt the moderate approach taken by my colleagues on this side of the House, especially that of the hon. member for Halton, who recognizes the constraints on government spending. He recognizes that these are difficult economic times and there is not enough money to pay for all the services we would like.
We have been cutting back in health, in transportation, and in mail service. Since 1975 there has been constraint on the letter carrier service. It has been applied fairly and equally across the country. It is a shame that people on one side of a street in a settled part of a city like Winnipeg, and certainly Toronto, have door to door delivery, while people on the other side of the street have to go to the box.
Governing the country is a difficult business, Mr. Speaker. All kinds of interests have to be reconciled. The one solution of the NDP is to throw money around. There are a lot more services that I would support if we had the money-pension increases, for instance. I notice that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is in the House. There are priorities, and we have to decide where to put our money. The Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) realizes that proper mail service is fundamental, but he is operating within the general constraints of the financial restraint program. There are social programs and other programs of the government which certainly deserve the money equally, or perhaps more.
